SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with Barney Bigard
by Patricia Willard
Reel One of Seven
1-4

Los Angeles, California
July 1976

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
MS. WILLARD: The interview with Barney Bigard, April 22, 1976.
Okay Barney
do you want to start back at the beginning? And I've found a couple of conflicting accounts in the John Milton book and in Leonard's Encyclopedia starting with your name.
Is it Leon Albany or Albany Leon?
Albany Leon Bigard.
Okay, which is -- that's the way John Milton has it.
Right.
And your birth date is correct, is it not? Because they both have it as March 3, 1906.
Right.
And you were born in New Orleans and Milton says on Villere Street. Is that right? V-i-l --
Villere.
Villere? Oh, it's pronounced Villere.
Yeah, V-i-l-l-e-r-e.
On Villere Street in New Orleans.
New Orleans, yes. That's known as the seventh ward.
Was there a specific address on Villere Street?
1726. I'll never forget it.
Did you live there long?

All my life. My grandfather, he bought this house and he bought another one and we all stayed there. And the house, the only time it ever changed hand is when my grandmother died. When he died nobody could touch the house until my grandmother died, and all the property was divided amongst his children, and so --
The house, is it still there in New Orleans?

No, it's gone now. It was so old and when she died they had so many children to be divided that they couldn't wait to get a decent price for it, so they had it up for auction. So they practically got nothing for it, and that's the way it went, a very cheap modest price. It was practically rotten.
And that's when well, I had I left on my 18th birthday and I went to Chicago to join King Oliver's band.

Oh.

What playing had you done in New Orleans?

Oh, I played with several bands. In fact, when I first started out we had a couple of fellows (instruments) that was learning -- one, by the name of Landry, was trying to play trumpet, and we had another guy trying to play drums. And it was all youngsters and we were all learning together at the

same time. We had about three tunes we could play, and one of them I'll never forget was 'The Sheik.' And so we used to go around [ ] for a Saturday and some of the people would have a party, a yard party, and we gave our services for nothing. We'd make them charge admission at the gate to come in and we'd take the proceeds and we'd wind up with a quarter apiece for the night's work. But we played those three pieces to death, every night.
(Laughter.)
It was fantastic. Yeah, we had a lot of fun.
How much was admission?
About 10 cents.
We had a lot of fun in those days and we enjoyed it. And it would give us a little experience, you know. And then, finally, I began to get better.

And my first big job with a big band was fantastic. That's the one with a fellow named Gaspard and they were looking for a clarinet player. And he used to -- he lived right near my home and he used to hear me every day practicing, so he asked my folks to let me come and play with them on a night job. So they didn't want me to go, anyways, so they -- he begged them, he said he'll take good care of me and bring me home. And one night they had a rehearsal trying to help me get started with the band, and the first piece they laid on me

was 'Tiger Rag.' And when they were finished I was still playing 'Tiger Rag.' That was very embarrassing because I couldn't get that two-four time. You see, I was reading like -- I played from my studies, you know. Four-four was four-four for me and so forth, but it was split time for dance music, you know. And I had a terrible time getting that in my head and especially 'Tiger Rag,' you know. It was so fast and they had all those clarinet breaks in there. Oh, boy. By the time you came to the breaks, they were gone and I was still fiddling around with the introduction.
Well, that went on.
Which did you play first, the clarinet or tenor saxophone?
The clarinet was my main instrument, but I was terrible. I was awful.
And then when the saxophone came out, then I began to play tenor so good and I took the soprano. And I played with the soprano and I didn't bother with the clarinet anymore. And I just --
When was --
-- put the clarinet down.
When was that that you were playing soprano?
The same time I started to playing the saxophone. I was not so good. That's when I went to
Chicago, you see.
Then when you joined King Oliver --
King Oliver.
-- you were playing --
Tenor.
-- soprano and tenor?
Right.
Oh.
And a friend of mine, Albert Nicholas, played clarinet. And when I joined Oliver, Albert Nicholas and Darnell Howard -- there was two clarinet players and --
Uh-huh.

-- they were in the group, so I -- and at the time they had music, if they had a little chorus, like for three clarinets, I'd play the soprano instead of the clarinet -- the part. So that's the way it went on. Then the guy wanted me to go to China.
What guy was that that wanted you to go?

A fellow from Chicago. He was taking the group to China. And I didn't want to go and I said, "No, I didn't want to go." So Albert Nicholas and Darnell went. said, "I'll go, I'll play tenor." So that left King Oliver with a lot of clarinet players, you know. So he came over to me one night, he said, "Didn't you use to play clarinet?" I said,

"Yeah, that's what I first learned." He said, "Why don't you play it?" I said, "Because I'm terrible." So he said, "If I buy you one, would you try to play it?" I said, "Sure. What have I got to lose?"

So he went downtown and bought one for me. And it was an old Conn clarinet, brand new, though. I took the thing home and (unintelligible) I started fooling around with it and I discovered that I could play more than I ever could on the clarinet. And I began to fool around with it and I began to like it again. And I woodshed -- you know, practicing -- we call it woodshedding, and I found out that it was coming around real good.

So he said, "You see, you little fool. You can play good. Why didn't you do that a long time ago?" I said, "Oh, I didn't like it like that. I didn't think I could do this kind of thing." So finally I started playing the clarinet and I put down the soprano altogether. The next thing you know I didn't want to play the tenor anymore. And so I kept on with the clarinet, and when I left Oliver and I came to New York -- and so I went to -- First I left Oliver and I went to Milwaukee with Charlie Elgar. He was from Chicago. He had a good band, too.
And I worked with Omer Simeon, and he's a fine clarinetist, too. Here's a boy that he really deserves a lot of praise but never did receive it, and he helped me a lot.
He showed me a lot of it that I had forgotten. And by working with him, and he was a real fine man.
Did he play the same system that you did?
Yes.
The Albert System.
Albert System.
Uh-huh.
And we got together, and then I really blossomed out. I began to blossom out real good. Then I stayed in Milwaukee all that year.
What year was that? Do you remember what year?
I can't remember because I left Oliver in about '25, I think it was. And we went to -- No, we came to New York. That's when I left Oliver.

We played the Savoy Ballroom and we had a battle with Chick Webb and Fletcher Henderson. And they wanted to hire Oliver at the Savoy for about four or five weeks but they didn't want to give him the money that he wanted. So we didn't have a job and we didn't have anything else to do. So then I got -- Luis Russell used to work with us, with me in New Orleans with Paul Barbarin and Willie Santiago and a trumpet player named Arnold Matwire.
Well, I've got to tell you this little story about

this Willie Santiago. He was the banjo player in New Orleans. You know, he used to come in at night and he'd sleep. He'd tune up his banjo and he'd go to sleep all night. Time to knock off or get off -- it was about ten to 15 minutes before we would knock off, he'd stretch himself and say, "Oh, boy, I feel good." And everybody in the band would say, "You should feel good. You slept all night."

And we'd go out and they had a club and everybody's turn -- whoever's turn it was -- they had to fill, they had what they call in those days a "cooler." They put ice in there and they'd fill it with wine and they had to cook the dinner for the club. And it was Willie's turn that night, that day, in fact, it was a Friday. So he went out and he bought a big fish, a big red snapper, filled the cooler full of wine, and he went out and got the fish when the market opened early in the morning, six o'clock. And he got stoned and he slept under a tree on [Claiborne] Avenue, it was the trees, and he went to sleep under the tree and the sun hit him and the fish. And they were talking about the flies, and everybody was just around looking at him and just laughing. And, boy, did they kid him about that. Oh, God, it was -- we used to have a lot of fun.
So then from then -- Then, getting back to New York, one night I went to work with Luis Russell at a place called The Nest Club, and I worked with Luis Russell for a long time.

And we used to go to work around ten o'clock till six, seven o'clock in the morning and we used to stay there and the big shots from Broadway would come in. All those big shots, like the stars, they called themselves, you know, fooling around in the morning and they'd come to the Nest and --
Who were the stars on Broadway then?

What's that girl? Helen Morgan. I can't think of all of them. Harry Richman. All them kind of people, and they called themselves, Browsing through Harlem, you know, and they come there and the boss was asking, "If anybody wants to stay, you can make some money playing for them people." You know, to entertain them.
And they'd come in there and they'd stay sometimes till 12, one o'clock.
The next day, till at noon?
[PAUSE]

Yeah, till at noon.) So we stayed there until sometime 12, one o'clock, and play for these people. And then I'd make my money -- my salary didn't mean a thing because I'd make more money than my salary. We'd just make more money. Sometimes we'd come out with $70, $80 tips from these people, and just that one night, one day.
What was the salary at that time?
Oh, salary. The salary was about $75, $80 -- No, $84. And we would make all -- that much in one night.
That's $84 a week?

Yeah, $84 a week, but we'd make almost that in tips sometimes. 75, 80. It depends on how they feel, you know. And then I stayed there. Then Charlie Johnson was the -- you see, we were supposed to be Charlie Johnson's second band because he was at Small's Paradise. And he got Luis Russell the job and Luis got the men.

And so that way -- and the funny part, one night I didn't understand the New York lingo with musicians at that time. So the boss came around -- he used to walk on the floors. He looked at me and said, "C'mon, boy, get off, get off, get off." So I thought he said get off the stand and I started packing my horn. He came back and said, "Where the hell you going?" I said, "I'm going home. You said get off." He says, "You dummy. I meant for you to take a chorus." He wanted me to jam a chorus. And everybody in the band started laughing. They didn't know what was happening, and after he told them, boy, they used to kid the devil out of me.

Well, anyway, that came on, and then I met Wellman Braud from New Orleans, but I didn't know him in New Orleans because he had been in New York practically -- oh, years before I ever got there. But he heard about me and all that, so he came around and him and I got to be real good friends. And he was working with Duke at the Cotton Club. Duke had just gotten a job at the Cotton Club and he was looking for a
clarinet player, a saxophone player, and Braud told him about me. So he told Braud to bring me over to his apartment. He wanted to see me.

So I went over there and his job was paying, at that time, was $72 or something a week. That's about all it was. But it was a big band, a ten-piece band at the time. So I went over to him and he acted like he was not so interested or nothing, you know, so Braud was telling me -- he used to call me "Millet" -- he said, "Millet, take it," he said, "I think it's going to be good because you can do a lot of recording and you can play different things and all that." He said, "If you don't like it, then you can quit."

So I gave my notice at the Nest. So the boss was telling me, "Why you want to leave?" He said, "You make more money here than going over there. I know what you're going to get over there." I said, "Yeah, but it's a -- I've got a good opportunity to make some more money, a bigger band," and all that. So they said, "Well, tell you what." They said, "If you don't like it, your job is always open for you here," so that gave me more courage to go anyhow. And I went and I joined Duke.
Was that in '27 or '28?
'27, the latter part of '27. And then I -- well, I'll continue that a little later on.
Okay.
But there's another subject I'd like to bring up while I'm at it.

I see all these critics are writing about New Orleans jazz, the Dixieland band, and all that. They don't know the half of what a Dixieland band is. See, the real Dixieland band, all of them, they had a violinist who was the leader, see. And the reason they had a violinist was because the average -- there was only about a few could read music, you know, like a trumpet player, a few good trumpet players that could read music. Very few clarinetists could read music. And trombonists -- very few trombonists could read music at that time.

So when they had a band, they had a violinist who was the leader. Like, he'd buy the music. He'd play the melody to the tune, whatever they bought, and then the trumpet player would pick up -- he'd pick up because he could play it, then the clarinet player, he'd listen and he'd put his own melody to it. So would the trombonist, see? And that's the way they formed the band, and that's how they got the melody.

But these people writing and they talk about -- they -- that's why they should give New Orleans' players a lot of credit, because in those days the whites wouldn't teach them. They wouldn't teach any colored guys to read music. They had to play it the best way they could. If they bought an instrument, they had to learn it the best way they could.
They'd finger instruments -- It's unbelievable the way they'd finger it, but they'd get the right notes. That's the greatest part about the whole bit.
Well, weren't there any colored music teachers or --
No.
None?

Only a few. That's what I said. Trumpet players, like Manuel Perez was a trumpet player, and they had some -- another good trumpet player, he was real light and he would pass for white and he wouldn't teach no colored at all.

Now, my teacher was Mexican. Tio, Lorenzo Tio. And his whole family was clarinet players from the great grandfather on down, the whole family. And his uncle -- we used to call him Papa Tio -- he was a better musician than his nephew, Lorenzo Tio. And he wouldn't take any -- he was a very peculiar man. If he'd take a pupil -- and the first lesson he'd give him and he could see that he wasn't going to be any good playing the clarinet, he'd tell him, "Son, I don't want your money." He said, "You want to be a clarinet player." He says, "Try something else." He said, "You don't have it." He'd tell them right off the bat. And nine times out of ten he was right.
But he took a liking to me. He took a liking to
Albert Nicholas and a couple of other guys. You see, as big as Sidney Bechet was, he couldn't read a note big as this whole house, and, like, he could play --
Did he ever read music?
No, the guy he could play though. Fantastic.
Did you ever know Sidney Bechet in New Orleans?
Sure. Oh, sure. Not in New Orleans.
Later?
Later. I met him in Chicago -- New York. I met him in New York first. And he's fantastic, He's great.
But that's a bit that a lot of people when they write they don't know what they're writing about, you know.
Were you a part of the music scene at all in New Orleans or did you become a part of the music scene when you got to Chicago?

I was just beginning to be a part of the music scene in New Orleans, but then when I got the opportunity to go to Chicago, then I went to Chicago. I went to join King Oliver. I had heard so much about him and I wanted to go and so I left then. But I was getting to be a part of the scene in New Orleans.
What musicians did you work with?

I worked with Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly. I worked with Manuel Perez. I had an opportunity to work with him. And I worked with Piron. Another fantastic trumpet man that nobody don't hear anything about is Amos White, and he's a professor at Berklee College of Music -- in music, a very fantastic man. He taught me a lot. And we had a band together and he took me around, and all these supposed to be big-time clarinetists like Picou, he showed me where they wasn't nothing. He did, too. Because he liked me and he was very interested in me, like my second father. He took good care of me. He taught me a lot of music, too.
I had a wonderful time, but I left. I was known as the "Slap Tongue King."
The "Slap Tongue King"?
Yes. Oh, I was good, but I started breaking too many reeds and it cost me, because it was too much money, I said, "I have to cut that out." And I left, and that's history.
How old were you when you started studying the clarinet?
Oh, I was about -- See, I studied music first. My uncle was a fiddle player, --
Oh.
-- and he taught me music, how to read

music. Then when I got to read music good, then I got -- in the band I used to play in, the clarinetist was Johnny Dodds. He used to play parades and he used to use an E-flat clarinet, the small one because I was too small to have the B-flat. My fingers wouldn't reach the holes, you know. So he borrowed the E-flat from him so I could learn and I started on the E-flat. And then it wasn't so difficult for me to learn the notes and learn the fingering. You see, I knew the notes but I had to learn the fingering. So when I got started that way, then when I began to grow a little bit -- well, I was about eight years old, nine years old -- then my fingers, when they got a little larger, then I got the B-flat clarinet. I bought that myself. That was my own, and I was proud. And my godmother used to make me a little velvet sack. That was my case. When I was going to take my lesson, I'd put it in my hip pocket, you know, or put it under my arm and let my girl see it, you know.
She say, "Where you going?" "I'm going to take my lesson." "What you got there?" "My clarinet." Oh, boy, I was something else.
Then my first --
(End of Proceedings as recorded.)
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with Barney Bigard
by Patricia Willard
Reel Two of Seven

Los Angeles, California
July 1976

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
How old were you when you bought your B-flat clarinet?

Oh, about 14 years old.
Now, this I have to tell you. You know, I had a friend, a good friend of mine, Big Eye Louie Nelson. He was a clarinet player. Usually people at clubs used to give picnics on Sundays out at Lake Pontchartrain and they'd hired him. And sometimes he'd be so tired he couldn't make it, so he'd get off and stop by the house and ask me to go and play in his place. So Zutty Singleton was in the band with Sidney Desvignes and all of them. And at the lake, you know, sometime the hall would be way out in the lake and you could walk up. They had a little walk path -- a little walk to get there, and when the wind would be blowing in, you could hear them talking, you know. It's like an echo.
So I was getting off the train and walking out there and Zutty spied me, you know. He said, "My God, look who that character sent out here today. That snake charmer." And, boy, and he says, "Oh, we're going to suffer today." So I didn't care, you know. I had a hard face because I was learning all the time, you know. And Zutty's uncle, a fellow played the banjo called Willie Bontemps -- and he's a very nice man -- and I had to sit next to him. So he says, "Son, don't pay them no mind." He says, "Do your best." He

says, 'Don't worry.' So we started playing some number and I was trying to jazz it up and I couldn't make them notes and the chord and I hit one note and I just held that note all the way, and Zutty said, 'Get off that damn note, get off. Cut that note off.' And I just held that note and I stopped that note so short. He hollered at me and I started almost to crying, and Willie put his arms around me. He said, 'Don't worry, son, I'll take care of you.' And every time I'd see Zutty we'd start laughing about that. I'd say, 'I'm going to hold that note on you when I catch you.'
(Laughter.)

He called me a snake charmer. Oh, we used to -- I had a lot of fun, though. But that's the only way I learned. I mean, I didn't care -- I mean, I played parades. Nine o'clock in the morning and playing in a parade till five in the evening.
The same parade?
Yes, 75 cents all day long.
A parade lasted from nine in the morning until five in the evening?
Yeah, sure.
What were the occasions for the parades?
Some club, like the longshoremen's
union or anything like that just walking. Labor Day, you know, they'd have about five or six bands, a big parade.
What -- you marched all over New Orleans?

All over, just walked. We'd stop and get something to eat and drink, and after they're finished and get a little rest, then they'd keep going and keep going. My feet looked like balloons when I got home. They're just soaking in hot water, cold water, hot water, cold water. Oh, boy. 75 cents. That's the kind of things that people -- I mean, kids nowadays don't know what hardship is, believe me.
How old were you when you started playing in parades?

About 14, 15. I was young, didn't care. I was just glad to be out and showing myself to the little girls, you know. All proud, you know. I had me a little hat, too, you know. Wear that rascal on the side. Sharp. I had a blue shirt, you know. The blue looked like denim and white pants. Oh, that was something. That was good, real nice.
And the parade was fun, too?
Oh, yeah.
It's a funny thing, when we used to play, like, play funerals, you know, and play a funeral -- that's a real kick. We played funerals and get to the grave,

the graveyard, and they buried most of the people in New Orleans in vaults, like in tombs, you know, because it's like swampland still, you know. They can't bury so deep because it's muddy and the soft mud and all that. So they make -- they called vaults, you know, and they play all this sad music going to the grave and they stand around when they put the character -- whoever died -- in the vault -- tomb, they call it, and seal him up. And the band turned around and come out and they say, "Ta-tat," and then the second line get together and all of a sudden they start out with "Didn't He Ramble" and, boy, then they start. Then they carry on and they dance all through the street, and at the second line, that's when the fun starts. Then everybody starts.

All those youngsters and even the crippled characters -- there was a guy called "Crip". He had one leg. He would be the leader sometimes, leading the second line on his peg leg. So it was a lot of fun.

I saw in -- I think it was what? -- Leonard says that you didn't want to be a musician but your family wanted you to be. Was that -- in Leonard's book? And then I read in Chilton that you worked with a photo engraver before becoming a musician?
I was a photo engraver.
Oh.
I was a cigar maker first.
A cigar maker?

Yeah. I was a cigar maker. See, I was starting used to work for my uncle first -- in the cigar business, and I started from the ground up. I started to strip tobacco, sift it, sweep the building, and I started to breaking bunches. Then I started to roll them. Then I started making them for myself. And then I went out in the big factory and I was working -- I started on the cheap job which sometimes was $8 a thousand. Then the big job was $50 a thousand. You had to be almost perfect, that when you roll them you could hardly see where you rolled -- how you rolled them. And sometimes you could only make about 15 a day, you know. 25 a day you got to be perfect.

And then the old men, they smoking cigars all through it. They didn't want no ventilation and they spit on the floor and the tobacco's on the floor and all that. And I saw all that and I began to get disgusted and sick of -- and I just quit.

Then I went to work for an old Russian named Romansky. He was a photo engraver and used to work for the newspaper. And I made more money working with him, making prints, you know, for the Sunday paper and all that, and I stayed with him for a couple of years. I was real good.
How old were you when you worked in the cigar factory?
Oh, I was about 11 or 12 years old.
And then when you went to work for Romansky?
Romansky, I was about 13, 14 years old. Then I began to study hard and liking music. But first I wanted to be a trumpet player.
Did you ever play the trumpet?

No. I tried it. I was coming along good, but only after I got big, you know, because my folks says, "Son, you don't have enough wind to blow the trumpet." And I could whistle good, so they decided to say, "Why don't you take up the clarinet?" And I said, "Well." They said, "Because you whistle good." And I said, "Well, I'll try it."
But I didn't care for the clarinet that much. I liked the trumpet better. But they didn't want me to take up trumpet. So I took clarinet, and that's what it was, clarinet.
Well, later when you tried playing the trumpet, did you think you would like it or not?

Well, I was too far gone on the clarinet then, you know, and I didn't want to start that trumpet all over again, so I -- if I did, I would just be just to play it a player like, probably like Benny Carter would, you know, [crossed out]. I wouldn't want to stay with it, I don't think. But otherwise, all right.
Had you known Joe Oliver in New

No. Oh, they were before my time. Well, he heard about me through -- Luis Russell left the band and he went to join King Oliver in Chicago. And then, the funny part, when I got to Chicago -- you see, Albert Nicholas went to Chicago. He left the group. We was working at Tom Anderson's for quite a while, just he and I, a duet, and the trumpet and -- but he didn't tell the man -- he was a Sneaky Pete -- he didn't tell the man he was going to leave, you know, because the man's business turned to bad and the man had to leave one of the musicians go. And I was the last one to join the group so they decided that it would be better for me, being the last one to come into the group, to be laid off.

So I got laid off. And the week I got laid off, that's when Albert took off for Chicago. So he left, and the boss was so angry that he didn't tell him that he was going to leave because he would never have fired me, you know. So he told the guys to go to my house and tell me to come back to work. I said, "I wouldn't come back to work for nothing in the world." So the guys told him I wouldn't come back to work.

So he came to my house himself and begged me to come back. I said, "No, I won't come back." He said, "I'll give you a raise." So he gave me a raise, gave me a $10 raise to come back. I said, "Okay," and I went back to work.
How much were you making then?
$25 a week. So I was making '35 a week, then, see? And that was big money in those days, you know. But our tips -- we had a kitty, and we was doing all right.
But Albert did dirty, you see. He was sneaky. He wouldn't tell the man, he said, "Well, I'm going to Chicago. Don't fire him." I don't know, he didn't tell the man that.
And then a little later on Luis Russell had Joe send for me. That's what he did.
Who was in King Oliver's band when you joined it?

Albert Nicholas, Darnell Howard, Paul Barbarin, Luis Russell, a tuba player named -- oh, what was his name? -- Cobb, Bert Cobb. And there was another Cobb playing -- No, Bud Scott playing banjo, the guitar. And a trombone player from New Orleans. I can't think of his name. He was a real nice man, though. I can't think of his name offhand. And that's about it. And, oh, yeah, another trumpet player. Oh, God -- I'll think about it. Oh, God, and I knew him well, too, a very fine musician. Skip it. I'll --
Okay. When you think of it we can drop it in anywhere.
Yeah.
When did you first hear the term 'jazz'?
Oh, I don't know. I heard it in so
many ways. They spelled it all kinds of ways. J-a-s-s and j-a-z-z and -- oh, I don't know.
But in New Orleans when you were coming up, was the term used in reference to the kind of music that was being played, or what was the music called?
Jazz.
It was called jazz?

(More like) They called it hot music. They called it hot stuff, hot music, jazz. And, you know, the funny part, I was telling my wife Dorothe that I didn't know Scott Joplin was a colored man. All them many years I didn't know he was a colored man. And my uncle used to send away for his books, you know, because he had all these -- like, for the band, you know, for instance, like for the trumpet, trombone, clarinet, and all that. He sent out for the set, Scott Joplin tunes.
Uh-huh.
I used to play them things. I'd always thought he was a white man. Never did know he was a colored man.
Because at that time there weren't many or weren't any colored composers with published works?
Not -- Only ones I knew was Piron, A. J. Piron and Clarence Williams.
Uh-huh.
That's the only ones I knew. I didn't
know Scott Joplin or W. C. Handy, none of them.
Handy's works were published then, were they?
No.
What -- I don't remember when they were first published.
No, neither was Jelly Roll's. Jelly Roll swore he's the composer of 'St. Louis Blues.' He said the old man stole it, he said, but since he made people think he did it, let him have the glory.
Do you think Jelly Roll wrote it?
Yeah, I think so. Excuse me.

Jelly Roll wrote a lot of things. Every time he wanted something he used to -- Melrose used to publish his pieces, you know, and every time he wanted $1,000, $2,000, or anything he'd write up a tune and give it to Melrose and say, 'Give me some advance money.' And that's how he used to get his money. And he had a diamond in his tooth in front there and he was a pimp, and he can talk himself into a job and talk himself out of it. He was quite a guy.
You knew him in New York?
I knew him -- Yeah, sure. He was quite a guy.
When did you start writing?
When I first started playing -- I didn't

even know what to do with them after I wrote them. I used to copyright my own tunes. I don't know what I did with the copyrights. And Paul Barbarin and I -- he used to stay at my house when he got off some show. And we had a little house back of our house that he and his wife lived in, and him and I, we'd sit in the back there and we'd dig up little ideas and I'd write them down and we sent to Washington to the copyright people and copyright them and put a name on. I don't know whatever happened to them.
There should be a record in Washington, shouldn't there?
I guess so, but that's been years ago. Those could be public domain, you know, after 28 years, is it? There were a lot of things.
What years do you suppose you started copyrighting tunes? Maybe this could be looked up.
No. Well, now, Duke -- you see, Duke did a lot of things. Duke, he put Harry Carney's name on "Rocking in Rhythm. Harry Carney never wrote a thing in his life, you know. That's true. I'm not kidding.
You mean Harry didn't have a -- Why did Duke put his name on it?
I don't know. He never did. And you know how that was -- come about, "Rocking in Rhythm?"
No, I don't know.

We was playing the Pearl Theater in Baltimore -- not in -- yeah, Baltimore, and these two comedians, they had a little thing about the numbers. They didn't have no music but they used to just stand up there, the two by themselves, and say, "We -- I got the number." "Where did you get it from?" Just them two. And so I started out, I said, "C'mon, Johnny, let's get something together." So I started out (humming), and Johnny fell in. A little later on Braud started in. Then after Braud started in, then Harry Carney finally found a little part (humming), and made the third part. That's how that started.
Do you remember who the comedians were?
Yeah, Johnny Lee and another little short guy. I can't think of his name. And they had that little thing going.
How long after you started playing behind them did Duke start playing it with the band?
Duke made an arrangement on it.
During that show?
Yeah, and I had to play the bridge in that (humming). Sure. Just like Lawrence Brown and Otto Hardwick, they made Sophisticated Lady.
How did that happen?
They were playing -- they were fooling
around in the dressing room in the theater, Lawrence Brown and Otto Hardwick. Duke made a tune out of it.
What did he do? Walk into the dressing room and hear it?
Sure, he would hear anything.
(Laughter.)

You see, that's what was bad about Duke. I mean, he didn't give the guys credit, you know, for what they did. He wanted to give everything -- like he did everything. People know that. I mean, -- he composed some good numbers, too. Give him that credit, but give the boys credit what they did, you know.
It's strange the way he wouldn't give credit where it was due yet give it to Harry when Harry didn't write.
He didn't do nothing. Harry never wrote a tune in his life. So that's where you are.
Well, I suppose this would be as good a time as any to talk about 'Mood Indigo'.
Oh, yeah, 'Mood Indigo'. He said he wrote that while he was having breakfast with his mother.
And actually what happened? I think you told me the story once before, but on this tape -- about 'Mood Indigo'.
Yeah. Yeah, he wrote the first part of
it (humming). He wrote that. But he didn't write the other part (humming). He didn't write that.
That was yours?
Uh-huh.
You wrote your part first and then he added --
Yeah, he added that part. He did that part. I give him that credit.
You wrote it and I think you told me once that you sold it to him. Is that right?
Yeah. We recorded it and Mills got hold of it, naturally, and then he gave me $25, and just by luck my name got on it, through ASCAP, and that's why I get royalties from it.
But didn't you say that it didn't get on it for a long, long time?
I didn't get on it for the first 28 years.
And there's no way of correcting that.
No. How about that?
Well, did you write it for a recording session?
Yeah, we did it for a recording session.
Was that the original name?
With my little group.
Oh. Which was called what? I think I have some 78's with your name --
It was called "Mood Indi-" -- BARNEY'S on the Syncopators, I think, that day they used to call me or something like that. Oh, well.
Well, your group was -- Was Barney's Syncopators a group out of the Ellington band?
Uh-huh.
Who was in that?
I think Whetsol and Tricky and myself, Duke and Sonny and -- about all. And they had another group with Tizol, Ben Webster, and somebody else was there. Its alright. Dottie?
(Unintelligible.)
Rex.
Rex.
Rex Stewart.
Yeah. Like the Man from "Lament for Javonette". That's mine. Do you know how I did that?
How?

At the Sherman Hotel in Chicago the girls used to dress like they were Javanese and they're selling cigarettes on the floor and the whole band is off, and I just sat up on the stage by myself on the bandstand and I just made up that little tune by myself. The next day we went to record it. Duke done put an introduction on it and fixed it up and dressed it up and put his name on it.
And dressed it up, how?
Added to it.
But did he keep the original name?
Yeah, "Javanette" -- "Lament for Javanette".
Because sometimes he would -- when he took something like that he would change the title.
No, he didn't change the title on that one. If there were any, he'd put his name on it. He'd put his name on to anything.

The guys gave him -- all the guys in the band gave him ideas, I mean, like if anybody stood up and took a solo, you know, and he heard something that he made playing that he liked, he'd tell them, "Play the solo. Play it again," until he got it. When he got it, then that's it. Then the next thing you know there's a tune coming out of it. That was Duke. He was clever, very clever. I won't take that away from him. The guy was clever.

But I -- Well, I say he should have given the guys credit for what they did. I mean, you know -- and he'll never -- he never would have a band like he had, his first band. Never. I don't care who he had in his band. You can tell from the old records -- I got a whole bunch of the old records -- and you hear the new records and you can forget them, and they got good men in the new records, I mean, but it's not the same band. And it's, like, people want to hear -- every time --
like he'd go to Europe, they want to hear what the old band did. They don't want to hear that new stuff he's trying to pull off, you know.
All those records that, those early records, they were immediately sold in Europe, weren't they?
Sure.
Yeah, so that there was a demand for the band right away.
Sure. They didn't care for that new stuff he was playing down there.
Well, we've got how many hours going?
(End of Proceedings as recorded.)
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with Barney Bigard
by Patricia Willard
Reel Three of Seven

Los Angeles, California
July 1976

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
June 23, 1976, and this is reel three of an interview with Barney Bigard.
Barney, on playing back the tapes we did earlier, I found a couple of questions I had.
One, you mentioned that when you first started playing in New Orleans that you played with somebody named Landry who played trumpet. What was Landry's first name?
Henry Landry.
Okay, and that was when you were just starting out?

Yeah. We were all kids together, just fooling around. And we used to -- every Saturday night we'd go find out who was giving a party or something and we'd play for the gate receipt. They'd charge them a quarter to come in, and so we'd wind up with about a dollar and a half or something like that for the whole night. And we had only about three pieces. 'The Sheik' was the main piece.
'The Sheik.' That's the same as 'the Sheik of Araby'?
Yeah, 'the Sheik of Araby.' And then the blues, and the third one was 'the Sheik'.
(Laughter.)
So we had two sheiks and the blues. That's all we could play, all night long.
Did Landry also become a professional musician?
No, he was nothing. He --
And you and Landry worked with a drummer?

Yeah, we worked with -- I can't think of the drummer's name. We were all kids. I mean, we didn't pay much attention to anything like that. We was out for fun more than anything else, which we did have a lot of fun.
You mentioned that you went with Gaspar's big band. What was his full name?
His full name was -- oh, God.
Well, maybe we can come back to that.
We'll come back to that. I'll think of it.
You mentioned, when you were talking about working in Chicago, that someone was trying to get a group to go to China and that was when you were working with Luis Russell?
With King Oliver.
With King Oliver. Who was it that went to China and who was it that was rounding up the --
Well, I was supposed to go. The guy wanted me to go to China and I didn't want to go to China, so
Albert Nicholas volunteered to go, and Darnell Howard, and those two went.
Was that as a part of a big band or a small band or --
Oh, he was taking a big group over there.
Who was it that was taking --
I can't think of the guy's name. He was a drummer, a famous drummer out of Chicago, and maybe later on I'll come back to his name.
Was a tour of China unusual in those days? Or did a musical group go to China often?
No, that was unusual. It took you about a month to get there because you only went there by boat or a ship or whatever you want to call it.
Well, this is the first time I've ever heard it mentioned, anyone going, any jazz musicians going to play in China. I've heard of lots of European trips, but was there a jazz audience in China or --

Oh, sure, and they had a pianist that used to play with Erskine Tate at the Vendome Theater in Chicago and he -- Teddy Wetherford. That was his name. I just happened to think of it. You see, it come back as we keep talking.
Uh-huh.
And he went over there and stayed over
there.
In China?
Yeah.
Playing?
Playing. Oh, he had a terrific audience over there.
Was there a lot of music being played in China, like jazz?
Not a lot. enough to keep him busy,
But not (inaudible).
That's why it went over so big because there wasn't so many.
Oh, I see.

And Darnell and Albert Nicholas stayed over there, oh, about two years or more, and they seemed to have enjoyed it, every bit of it, because I used to see his father. His father came to New York when I was there -- Albert's father -- and every time he got a letter from Albert, Albert was telling him how great they were doing and how much money and everything and had more diamond rings and all that sort of business. And when he came back to the states he didn't have a quarter, and that was really funny.
Could we put the mike a little closer? (Inaudible.)
So I had to take him down to the music shop there where they were selling horns and I knew the guy
real well, and I'd take him down there and I got him a set of instruments. And then Luis Russell had a band, so he took Albert Nicholas to work with him in his band and give him a break.
Well, did Albert Nicholas work steadily for two years in China?
Yeah.
There was that much work?
It was --
In China?

-- a big -- It was a hotel they were playing, a big hotel, like the Shanghai Hotel or something like that and they did very well over there. They had servants in -- they were so cheap. I mean, they hired cooks and everything for their apartment. Oh, they had everything. That's why they loved it so much, you know. But it turned out all right.
But his old man was very disappointed when he came back to the states and didn't have a quarter.
What happened to it?
Oh, who knows what happened?
You mentioned that you had an uncle who was a fiddle player. That was --
Emile.
Emile?
Emile Bigard.
And -- Big Eye you said?
Bigard. Bigard, just like mine.
Emile Bigard. I see.
Yeah.
And was that the same uncle or a different uncle who also was a cigar maker?
It's another uncle that was a cigar maker.
What was his name?
Ulysses Bigard.
You see, in New Orleans, naturally the American people say Bigard, but in New Orleans' patois they call it Bigard.
Oh.
That's half French -- a piece of French and whatever. It's Bigard.
I see.
And my whole name is Albade Leon Bigard.
Which sounds very French, but yet,--
It is French.
-- on the other hand, you pronounced the name of the street where you were born --
Villere.
-- Villere rather than the French pronunciation.
That's the only pronunciation for that street, is Villere.
Oh, I see. So there were both French pronunciation and Americanized pronunciation for French words, in New Orleans.

Yeah. Well, the American -- they never used it -- You see, like New Orleans was divided. Canal Street divided -- they used to say the American part of Louisiana and from American down was the Creole section, which was the half French. You know, the patois French.
Uh-huh.
And that's the way it was, and so they never really got together too much.
Do you speak French?
Yeah, I speak a little.
Do you speak any other language besides French?

No, only what I want to speak when I go in them different countries and when I want something or get some guy to tell me what I'd like, to go to a restaurant or a taxi, take him in a taxi till I get the layout of how much money I should give him, you know, whatever -- pesos or whatever. And things like that. But I can speak a lot of French. All my people were French. They couldn't speak English at all.
So French was spoken in your home?
Oh, yes.
When you were growing up?
See, they couldn't speak English at all.
Oh.
They went to an all-French school. I got some French books right there I'll show you a little later on from my grandmother. You can pull those three down there. See down there? Yeah.
yes they look very old.
Oh, (inaudible).
That's my grandmother's book, -- 'L'Histoire Roman'.
(inaudible)
-- and they're all written in French.
But how many generations back? Did your grandmother come from --
That's my grand --
-- France?
Huh?
Did your grandmother come from France? Or how many generations --
My grandfather came from France.
Grandfather.
He came from Lisle, France.
Oh, when -- at what point in his life? When he was a child or --
No, when he was a young man. Then he

came over to the United States and he met my grandmother in -- I think in Mississippi somewhere, of all places, and they got married. And she spoke a lot of French. She was French, too, where she came from, but he met her in Mississippi, you know.
Uh-huh. What was your grandfather's name?

Emile, Emile Bigard. And I had my uncle, was Ulyssis, and my father was Alexander. And Emile is from -- you see, my grandfather, that was his second wife -- my grandmother. And Emile is her son, see? So they were like stepsons with the rest of the family. Then I had my godmother, my father's sister named Louise.
Your father's sister was your godmother?
Huh?
Your father's sister was your godmother?
Yeah.
Did she raise you, because Dottie --
My grandmother raised me because my mother died when I was born, at my birth. Dottie was telling me that
So your household consisted of whom then? man?
Yeah.
You lived with your grandparents -- your grandmother and your grandfather -- and who else?
And that's all, my uncles and my brother.
My mother's name was Emmanuela and my grandmother's name was Eugenia.
Which grandmother? Was that your --
The one that raised me.
Was that Emile's wife?
Emile's mother -- Emile was my grandfather.
Yeah.
It was his wife.
Uh-huh, and (inaudible). They had a son, Emile.
And his son, Emile Jr., from my grandmother.
And you had what, one brother?
I have two brothers.
Two brothers. One was named A MUSICIAN.
One was Alec, Alexander, he was a drummer. He's still a drummer but he's in a bad way. He can't hear and so he can't work. [PAUSE]
We were talking about your brother Alec. Where does he live now?
He lives in New Orleans.
I see. Oh, yeah.
And he's old, you know. He's older than
I am, naturally.
How much older is he than you?
Oh, he's about in his eighties now. And he can't hear, because if he could hear, he could always play and make some money. So he's living off Social Security and food stamps and things like that.
Did you ever play together?
No.
No?
No, we could never play together.
Why?
Because he can't play like I like to hear drums. He's a terrible drummer. To me --
And -- Huh?
He's a terrible drummer for me. I couldn't play with him. We'd probably be like Jimmy Dorsey and Tommy Dorsey, fighting all the time.
You had another brother?
I had another -- Sidney, yes. Well, he was killed. He was shot. He and some other guy were fighting over his wife. That's a long time ago.
Did he ever play music?
No. No, he was a hard worker, just all labor.
But I never got to tell you about my earlier days
No.
No? I got to --
A little bit on that first tape about --
Yeah.
Well, my early days were fantastic, you know, because every time I look back on it, I think about it -- I think I told you about Buddy Petit and all that.
You mentioned having worked with him.
Yeah.
But you didn't tell me much about him.
Buddy Petit was a strange character.

You know, in New Orleans they didn't have any union musicians for colored people. So they'd take jobs and get a deposit. And Buddy Petit was very popular at that time, and he'd take all the jobs he could to get the deposit to go and drink.

Well, I was a youngster and I didn't -- I got in on the tail end of his career and the beginning of mine. So they had -- every year the longshoremen, they gave a big picnic in a big lake, a big party with all the different unions. And I happened to be working with him at that time, and we were doing good and playing pretty good. I was scuffling like as usual because I didn't know much about it. So there was a cop stationed on the bandstand. So when we had finished a set, the cop asked some of the guys in the band, he says, "Who's Buddy
Petit?" And one boy would say, "The trumpet man right there. That man." So the cop would say, "Oh, that can't be Buddy Petit." He says, "Don't tell me that can't be Buddy Petit. That's Buddy Petit."

So we finished the next set and he's getting ready to go off the stand and the cop stopped him and says, "Somebody said you're Buddy Petit." He said -- he stuttered, incidentally, you know -- he said, "Th-th-th-th-th-that's me. I'm Buddy Petit. There's only, only one." The cop says, "Oh, c'mon, man, you're not Buddy Petit." He says, "Don-don-don-don't tell me I'm not Buddy Petit," and he reached in his inside coat pocket and pulled out a gang of contracts with his name, you know, and he said, "W-w-w-w-w-what that say there, huh? Don't that say B-b-b-b-b-Buddy Petit?" The cop says, "It does say Buddy Petit. Well, come with me," and took him to jail.
Oh.

So they had sued him for all the contracts that a lot of people had sued him and he hadn't showed up, and he would send some -- any band, anybody he could find -- on that job, and the people wanted -- well, his name was so big he drew a lot of people, you know, like especially if they gave a dance or whatever it was. So we played without our trumpet all the rest of the night and that was awful.
So it went on like that.
You mentioned that your uncle taught you music, your --
Yeah.
Was he the one who taught you the clarinet fingering?
No, no, no.
Who taught you that?

You see, he taught me how to read the music and the division of the bars and all that. I had a book, you see. And he taught me that. Then when he found out that I could do pretty well like that, they didn't give me a clarinet at all to start with, which I am very happy until this day, you know, because that would have been double -- you know, like, too much for my little brain to manipulate, trying to read the music, and the fingering of the clarinet. And then my hands were so small, and so they used an E-flat, what they call an E-flat clarinet, to play parades with, the brass band, because they're shrill. They can make a lot of noise, you know.

And so the guy that played in his band was Johnny Dodds. He played clarinet in his band, and he had one, so my uncle borrowed his E-flat. Yeah, so he borrowed -- he loaned my uncle his little E-flat clarinet since he wasn't playing in many parades. And only I'd give it back to him when he had a parade to play. And then my little fingers could fit the keys and the holes or whatever. And they got one of the
best clarinetists in New Orleans at that time, the great, as far as I'm concerned, Lorenzo Tio, and he played with A. J. Piron's society band at Trenchina's at Spanish Fort.

And he began to give me lessons. Then Piron had a deal to go -- the first southern big band to go to New York to play at the Roselond Ballroom. So Lorenzo Tio -- his uncle was a great clarinetist because the whole family, all the men from the great-grandfather on down, were all clarinetists, magnificent clarinetists. And the old man, he didn't want to be bothered with pupils anymore because he couldn't stand them if they couldn't do what he wanted them to do. They'd make him nervous.

But Lorenzo, his nephew, begged him to take me because he said he saw possibilities in me. So the old man said, "Okay. Well, send him on." So I went to him, and the old man liked me. And he taught me the rest of the way.
So your very first instruction --
Huh?
Your very first actual instruction on the clarinet was from Lorenzo Tio?
Yeah, he was my first teacher, which I was very lucky.
Uh-huh.
And that's how the thing went on. And when he said, "Well, now, son, I've taught you." He says, "I

know you want to go out and play music if you feel like it. What kind do you want to play?" And I told him, "I liked the jazz, that fancy music." And we used to have -- he had a band at the club they belonged to like a little symphony band, you know. The old man, and he was the conductor and he used to ask me to come and sit and play with them.
With the little symphony band?

Yeah. But I didn't like that. But it was good for my reading, you know. But then when I went to go to play jazz then it was a different story altogether. I had to divide my music, what I had learned. I had to divide the time, the tempo, and I was getting kind of disgusted, but then I kept at it. I really kept at it for a while.

Then I went, I got a job with some guy in -- he had a job around Oswego somewhere in some kind of club. So one night the boss came in and says, "Where's that damn snake charmer?" And say, "There's no snake charmer here." He says, "I hear that one note. Who's holding that damn one note in my place here?" So he told the guy, "Get rid of him."
(Laughter.)
So I was fired that night, bam, and I said, "Oh, well."

So then the soprano came out, the soprano saxophone, and I kind of liked that. And I got the tenor first but then I'd take the part of the clarinet because the music was written, like, another chorus would be for clarinet and one would, you

know, the sax. And I kind of liked that so I got that and I put the clarinet down and forgot all about it till I went to Chicago, and that's when Albert and Darnell left to go to China. I wouldn't go.

And King Oliver -- I told you about King Oliver buying me this clarinet. He asked me did I play it. I said, "Well, yes." He says, "Well, if I get you one, will you try?" I said, "Sure, I'll try. What have I got to lose?" And he got it and I started woodshedding, and I started to thinking, "Well, gee, I can play more than I ever did play," I mean, you know. And I kept going at it like that. Then I began to like that better than I did sax, and so I just kept at it, and that's the way it is. I don't play sax anymore.
You never played saxophone again after that?
No, I won't play it. I don't like it anymore. And so that's the way that happened.
How long did the nickname "snake charmer" stick with you? Because you mentioned it on the other tape in a different context.
Yeah. Oh, that lasted a long time.
How long?
As long as I was in New Orleans.
But, you know, when I got the sax then I learned how to what they call "slap tongue." You see, in Piron's big band
he had an alto player called Louie Warnecke and he was the first one I ever heard do that slap tongue business.
Which is what exactly?

You pop the reed; instead of making a noise, you have "pop," just like you pop, like you slap anything flat, you know. And so he taught me and I kept practicing at it, practicing. Then they called me the "King of the Slap Tongue." Then I got more work than I could ever handle. And all the guys that fired me and did me dirt, I says, "I'll get even with them." I'd take the job and I wouldn't go on it.
(Laughter.)
I had a lot of fun.
So you had another nickname, the "King of the Slap Tongue."
You mentioned in New York that Wellman Braud called you Millet, Miyai?
Millet.
Millet. How do you spell -- ?
I don't know how you spell it. It's --
Millet.
Millet. That's a nickname for anybody, I guess, from New Orleans.
Oh.
See, I didn't know Braud in New Orleans

at all, only when I -- I knew he was from New Orleans when I got to New York because somebody had told him about this boy from New Orleans in the band with King Oliver, and all that, so he came over and we got acquainted. He got to be my best friend. He looked out for me in New York. I mean, because he had been in New York long years, and he looked out for me and he saw that nothing would happen to me. In fact, he guided me right. He was like my father, you know. And we were real thick, real thick friends.
Was it he who started calling you Millet?
Yeah, Millet.
Millet?
Millet. Hey, Millet.
I remember we got to Duke's band -- and that's one thing I didn't think Duke liked because he didn't know what we were talking about half of the time.
(Laughing.)
So --
Did you have any other nickname?
No, that's all I had. "Snake Charmer" was the main one, and that was the main one, and Millet was -- that was between Braud and I.
But I did all right, though, in -- I enjoyed -- I used to play -- Honest to God, I played parades from nine
o'clock in the morning till five in the evening for 75 cents, walking. And when I'd get home, I'd get a tub of hot water to soak my feet in and go right to bed. Boy, --
That was in New Orleans. I think you mentioned before that there was a trumpet player in New Orleans who passed for white and wouldn't take any colored music students. Do you remember his name?
It was -- yeah, his brother was a clarinet player, too. He was in Philadelphia the last time I saw him. Oh, God. You're bringing back some real oldies on me now.
Okay, we'll make notes of these when we come back. Maybe they'll come back a little later on.
Yeah, --
I know we're kind of jumping around from --
Pillar to post, yeah. I can't think of his name right now. It'll probably come to me as we're talking.
Okay. Well, back in New York, you mentioned that Braud took you to Duke's apartment. Where was Duke living then (unintelligible), when he took you there to talk about joining Duke?
Joining the band.
Uh-huh.

He was living on Seventh Avenue somewhere, around there, in one of those apartment buildings. And I didn't know his wife had cut him -- that big scar he had on the side of his face? His wife had did that to him.
That was Edna, right?
Yeah.
That was back in Washington, right?
Yeah.
And she never came to New York, did she?
Oh, sure.
She did?
Sure.
When did she come to New York?

Oh, she was there when I was there. I got there -- well, I joined Duke in '27 and I'd been in New York about -- in '25, and I saw her then because I was working with Luis Russell at the place called the Nest.
Where was that?
That's on Seventh Avenue and -- oh, right around the corner from -- there was a famous theater. Well, I'll say right around the corner from Connie's Inn. The Nest was like an after-hour joint.
Uh-huh.
That's where I made more money, at the Nest, than I made on the regular job, just staying there playing for the -- big shots used to come after their show off Broadway.
Did you have a regular job in addition to the job at the Nest; at the same time?
Sure.
What was your regular job?
It was at the Nest.
Oh.
That was the regular job but --
And then you also played there after hours?
Yeah, we stayed there.
I see.

The boss said if you wanted to make some money, you can stay there and make some money because they'd tip, you know. Helen Morgan and all those kind of people used to come there. And they'd have a ball -- sometimes I wouldn't get home till 12 at noon. But I had me about 40 or $50 in my pocket, too. And my job only paid me about 75. That's right.
And you left that --
And I left all that to go with Duke.
Whom I think you said was paying less

Oh, yeah. So the boss (at the Nest) said -- well, he tried to discourage me from going. Well, I said I got to try it anyway. So he said, "Well, if you're not satisfied, you're job is always waiting for you."
Did you ever --
So I said, --
-- think about going back?
-- "Thank you." No.

After I got to working in a big band, and I kind of liked it, and Braud kept telling me, "Millet, this guy's going to go places. We're going to make some money. Stay. Don't leave. Stay." And I stayed and we did make money. He told me right.
Did Edna go back to Washington somewhere along the --
Oh, she used to go back and forth all the time.
Was she in Washington when you took up with Mildred Dixon or was she still in New York?
She was in New York. She was a -- I never knew much about Edna.
(Unintelligible)
No, she was an evil -- But Mildred is a cute little gal. She's cute. She was real nice. She used
to dance with a fellow called Henry --
I think -- (Inaudible) it ought to be in Vianen's book,
Uh-huh.
But -- yeah, well, they were partners anyway and she used to dance with him. I'll think of that -- it had come along from the Cotton Club show.
Uh-huh.
Ah --
Do you know what it was that Duke did that got him cut?

No. I don't know what happened. But, see, that was way after -- She cut him way before I knew him and I didn't know what -- But then I know she used to -- I heard. I don't like to mention names, I mean, because it wouldn't be nice. So I'll be discreet.
Well, you can --

But he was quite a figure in the music world. That's all I'll say, and a real gentleman. That's about it. And I imagine Duke heard about it and got after her and they had a big argument and she waited till he went to sleep and slit him on his face with a razor blade.
I think the dancer that Mildred did some dances with was Henry Wesson.
Henry Wesson? that's it.
That's what it says in Barry Vianen's book.
(Inaudible)
What a wonderful guy.
So they were dancing at the Cotton Club?
Yeah.
And that's where she and Duke met?
Yeah.
And that was --

She saved Duke. Duke used to gamble, you know, and sometimes he didn't have enough money to pay off the boys in the band and she'd give him her salary to pay off. And he treated her badly. He was terrible.
They were together about 10 years, weren't they?
Pretty long, but I don't think 10 years, no. But they were a long time together.
Until he took up with Bea?
Yeah. That's later.
Was that when he left Mildred, was when he met Bea?

Yeah, well, they fell out, and when the Cotton Club moved down to Broadway, that's when he took up with Bea. And Bea used to be with -- oh, God. He was out here. He was the emcee and everything. He looked like a white boy and he stayed, lived mostly out in Pasadena. He was the emcee at the Apollo Theater.
Leonard Reed?
Not Leonard.
Willie Bryant?
Willie Bryant.
She had gone with him before?

Oh, yeah. He used to beat the beJesus out of her. And he didn't have any prize there, you know, because she -- she went with Joe Louis at one time and I caught her in Detroit with Joe Louis. She was no prize at all.
But yet he kept her as a housekeeper to the end?
Yeah, he kept her. What else he's going to do?
And Duke was a coward. He'd do all his dirty work and he'd have a guy, like, in Washington called "Weak Knees," a bad guy, and he'd have him protecting him all the time when he was in Washington.
He had a bodyguard named "Weak Knees"?
"Weak Knees." Yeah, in Washington, D.C. But Jonesy -- Jonesy used to -- his valet, he used to watch after him, too.

At one time he had me -- he tricked me into having a breakfast with him because he thought -- he didn't tell me until after -- he thought this guy was going to come in the restaurant and beat him (up) and so I was supposed to be the bodyguard.
He always had to have a lot of intrigue around him, --
Yeah.
-- even if he had to create it himself on purpose, just to keep things stirred up.
He was something else. I wanted to beat him one time.
You what?
I almost beat him.
What happened?
I had him by the neck and the head and I was getting ready to smash him.
What had happened?
Huh?
What were you mad about?
He interfered in my love life. I told him, 'Cut it out.'
He always did that with the members of the band, didn't he? He always tried to --
Yeah.
-- mind everybody's business.

Show somebody how to do, what to do, and what not to. You see, I'm a man. I'm like you. I don't tell you what to do. And one word led to another and I just grabbed him and I was going to whack him, and one of the guys -- I
think it was Cootie -- grabbed my arm and I just threw him up in the corner or something.
Did anybody ever get so mad that they hit him or beat him that you know of?

No, no, not that I know of. I tell you, see, it doesn't pay to hit a man like that because he's a big shot and you're a little, like the little frog in the pond, you know. And so I said, "Oh, forget it." I think Tizol wanted to cut him once, I think. I don't know. He was something else. But all in all, he was great. I liked Duke till he started stealing tunes. You know, he was all right.
I know you told me --

But the thing that mostly when I got really disgusted with him -- see, he, every time somebody, a friend of his died, he'd go around to the guys and ask them if they want to donate a little money for flowers or something to send to this guy's wife, or if he was stranded, if you want to make a little pot to give him and let him go home. And when my father died, I was in Chicago, and he had met my father. I told him, I said, "Duke, my dad died," I said. So we got together and, he'd you know, "make -- send some flowers down there," you know. Nothing. He didn't say nothing like this -- everything -- that teed me off but good, because

if I could give money to friends of his, people that I don't know, and he knew my father and I'm working for him, you know, then I thought that he should reciprocate, in a way, that -- to try to help make me feel halfway good anyhow. So I didn't say no more about it, but I never did forgive him for it and I never did care for him anymore.
You told me about 'Mood Indigo', that -- did he take any other music of yours that you didn't get credit for?
Oh, I got about 13 tunes. You'll see them on that thing I gave you --
The discography?
-- to look at. Yeah, that discog -- whatever you -- what do you call it?
Discography.
Yeah, discography. You'll see my name on them. I never did get credit for it. I had about 13.
And these are all things that Duke put his name on
'Saturday Night Function', Check and Doublecheck' -- not 'Check and Doublecheck' 'Rocking in Rhythm' -- he put Harry's name on there.
And you said Harry didn't make any contribution?

Nothing, he couldn't compose a note. He didn't know nothing. Harry couldn't compose nothing if he tried, God bless his soul. He's a good boy, but he couldn't compose nothing. Well, he did that because Harry was riding him around.
Harry was a very devoted subject?
Yeah.
And he -- I don't think he ever got over the father-son kind of a feeling that he had for Duke. I mean, he acted -- he really did treat him like --
Yeah.
And Duke sort of disciplined him as though he were his son. They had a --
Well, Duke didn't -- he treated his son awful, terrible. He thought more of his sister than his son.
Well, his sister is the only one who could no wrong, isn't she?
Is what?
Is the only one who could do no wrong? I mean, --
Yeah.
-- Ruth was always perfect.
Yeah, with the mother and the father and Duke, because anything his mother would say, that was it, because he was madly in love with his mother, which is wonderful.
But Ruth --

Do you know if it's true that the reason he hated brown so much in later years, the color brown, was because he was wearing a brown suit the day his mother died? I've heard that story. You know if it's true?
No, I don't. I've never heard nothing like that.

He had (unintelligible) very strong feelings against the colors brown, yellow, and green. He didn't like them. And somebody told me that brown was because that's what he was wearing the day his mother died.
Oh, that's a story, because he had some brown clothes.
But not in later years.
I don't know about the later years.

In later years everything was blue or variations of blue, red, purple, white, black. But no brown, no green, no yellow. And he didn't want anyone to wear those colors around him and he would tell them so. He would order them to change their clothes if they came around in those colors. But he didn't have those prejudices back when you were with him?
No. He wouldn't fool with me no-how. He didn't trust me.
Where did he get the nickname Dumpy?
I don't know. I think from Freddie Guy. I think he got that from him, him and Sonny Greer.
Because I know you called him Dumpy sometimes, or Dump, didn't you?
Yeah, I called him that. He don't like that name. I used to call it to him anyhow, bam. So let's cool it for a while. [PAUSE]
I've heard it said that Duke Ellington never fired anybody. Is that true?

That's true, but he made it so miserable. If he wanted somebody to leave, he made them so miserable that if they had any kind of pride within themselves, that they would just quit, and that would satisfy his ego and it kept his record clear that he's never fired anybody.
I saw that in operation with Rufus Jones in later years when he finally got to quit. Whom did he use it on earlier?

Oh, well, he couldn't do it -- he wanted to do it on Bubber Miley so much but he couldn't because Bubber Miley was the stylist for the band at that time. And he wanted to do it on Otto Hardwick but Otto Hardwick was one of the originals of the Ellington band. So that's about all. Then he got bold and he gave Freddie Guy a bad time and so Freddie just quit, and he -- I think he actually fired
Sonny because, well, Sonny wasn't doing the job. I mean, he was -- he stayed stoned all the time and he had to eventually fire him or something because he wouldn't straighten up --
That was around 1950, wasn't that?
Yeah, because he couldn't do his job. But the guy that he got was just as bad as Sonny. What's that? -- Woodward, Woodyard?
Sam Woodyard.
Yeah. Oh, God.
He didn't start until 1955. There was a whole succession of drummers.
Well, I know, but they didn't cut the mustard.
He liked Louie Bellson but --
Yeah.
-- he couldn't keep him because -- well, Pearl got Louie to quit.
Oh, sure.
And there was Charlie Smith and Dave Black and Butch Ballard and a half a dozen more between Sonny and Sam Woodyard.

Oh, yeah, there was a bunch of them. They couldn't -- well, they couldn't cut the mustard, I mean. Bellson was one that did a good job. Well, he knew what he was doing and, naturally, he was looking out for himself, too, he
and Pearlie Mae was -- so I knew that wasn't going to last long, which it didn't. But every now and then he'd go out and help Duke. He helped Duke out when he got a chance.
Well, Louie was very devoted to Duke.
Yeah.
And Duke
He maintained that Pearlie Mae only married him, only married Louie in order to rob Duke of a drummer.
Oh.
He got very paranoid in later years. Was he -- Did he used to be like that? Did he used to --

No. That's what I said. Well, I thought that -- to me he got more senile than anything else, not paranoid, because I've never known him to act like he did on the end of his life there, the way he was doing, the things that he was doing.

And every time I saw him he would want to grab me and hug me, you know. And then the last time -- the time that I was teed off on him was at the concert at Carnegie Hall when he was supposed to introduce some of his past musicians in his band. You know, for the Newport Jazz Festival.
That was in '75, was it?
Yeah, and --
No, '73, I guess it must have been because he died in '74. It must have been 1973.

Well, -- which was George Wein's idea that he'd like to reminisce, you know, get a few of his men that was in the group, like Sonny, Nance, myself, and somebody else, I don't know. And so George told me, "Get here a little early because Duke is coming in early." He had been working somewhere. I don't know, it was somewhere in Jersey somewhere. And he was coming in for a rehearsal with Nance and Sonny and myself. And so I said, "Okay."

So I came in early and there he was. So he started rehearsing things that he had been playing, I mean, probably all that night. So he said, "What you want to do?" I said, "I'll do something simple." He said, "How about 'Tiger Rag'?" I said, "You must be kidding. 'Tiger Rag'. It's hard. I said simple. Don't you know what simple means?" So he said, "What?" I said, "Rose Room." I said, "Everybody knows 'Rose Room.'" So he said, "Okay." He said, "What tempo?" I said, "You know the right tempo," and I gave him the tempo. So I told him what I wanted and his drummer -- you know where he kept the drummer way up on something. And I'd do little diddles after I'd finish the chorus and the drummer was supposed to follow, you know. So I didn't care, so I said, "Okay."

So that night Sonny was there, Ray Nance was all dressed up, bless his soul, and he had his fiddle. And he was talking about -- Ray Nance was talking to me about Duke had did him something and he was threatened by the guy that -- whoever
he had was his boy. I mean, his valet.
At that point it was Jim Lowe?

I don't know who it was -- to beat up Nance and Nance said, "I wished they would. Anyone" -- he and his son. And Duke was in the room getting his legs shaked down by this guy, (Ray so) Nance said, "Yeah, I wish any one of them would come out there."

So when the curtain went up for the concert, Sonny was downstairs. They called me down. I came down and I sat. And Duke was announcing. So all of a sudden he called, "Here's the great Greer." And that's all. The boy hadn't gotten off the drums yet. Sonny had to climb up on that stage to get on the drums and Duke said, "We're going to do a little something we did together for a while." And Sonny was trying to ask him, "What are you going to play? What are you going to do?" He said, "That's all right. Just follow." So Duke started playing anything and Sonny was just fooling with the drums and hitting the cymbals. And first thing, you know, Duke said, "Oh, that's enough of that," and then went back to the mike, left Sonny up there. Sonny had to hop down off that stage to get back out. And that's all he said about Sonny.

I said, "What is this business?" So I sat there and he turned around to look, to see, and he saw me there and he saw me looking at him, and all he says then, "And now I'd like to introduce one of my fine clarinetists I had in the band, Barney

Bigard." Boom, that was it.
He got up there so I started -- he gave an introduction, playing the tune, and he's playing it slow, like a drag. And now it's getting to be sixteen -- and I said, "No, keep your cool. Just go ahead and bear with it." And I'm trying to get him to pick it up, pick up -- but he can't get to him. He don't want to see that at all. Okay, so I go through and the thing was -- the people, whatever it was, they liked it anyway, and I could have taken an encore or anything. That was it. So I said, "Well, that's fine."

So now Nance is in the wings all dressed up and his fiddle's raring to go. He never did call Nance. Never. I said, "Well, I'll be darned." And he had some old funny singers -- I don't know whether they were European singers or what. Girls, a couple of girls or something like that. Did you know that?
I know there was one girl he brought from, I think, Scandinavia and another one from Canada.
Yeah, there was that -- it didn't mean a thing, absolutely nothing.
One was very good and one was terrible.
Uh-huh.
was the opinion I heard.
So, I mean, and that's what happened.
And I said, "What is with this man?"
Well, he did a lot of strange things, like he got Norris Turney to quit by doubling the tempo behind him on his solos. Now, you say he played too slowly for you.
Uh-huh.

He played so fast as to try to, I guess, make it too fast for Norris to be able to play, and I was told by members of the band that Norris, right in the middle of his own number, closed up his instruments in their cases and walked off the stand, and that was when he quit because he was doing it to him.
Uh-huh.

And that was, you know, in later years. And several of the people -- he would tell the singers, whoever they were, in the band, and one time he told Tony Watkins that he should call home and tell his relatives in Philadelphia that he would be on, I think it was the Merv Griffin show -- some television show Duke was doing. And Tony should be sure and wear his tuxedo to the television station because Duke wanted to really put on a nice performance.
So Tony did. He alerted all his relatives. And then he was kept standing in the wings, like you say Ray Nance was. Duke never even acknowledged the fact that he was there and he was never on.
Oh, he got terrible.
Tell me about Mexico in New York.
Oh, Mexico was funny. When I first went to New York, Mexico was a speakeasy joint, you know, and --
Where was it?
On -- right near where, oh, -- oh, God. You heard of the Lafayette Theater, huh?
Yes.
That's on Seventh and --
I can't remember where.
Well, --
Tom Whaley told me (Inaudible) about the Lafayette Theater.
Yeah, well, it was right around the corner from the Lafayette Theater but it was down in the basement.

So in those days they used to call them "cutting contests." You know, like instead of a jam session. So I had just gotten to -- I hadn't been in New York long -- so Luis Russell told me, he said, "C'mon, we're going to go into the cutting contest." I said, "What do you mean, cutting contest?" He said, "You'll see."

And this night was piano night. James P. Johnson, Willie the Lion. They had Duke in there and Fats Waller. All the biggies, you know. And Mexico had his little bar and on the back of the bar was all the hammers to hit the strings, you know, in the piano, because when the Lion would get up there,
he'd -- the Lion's going to roar and he'd bang the piano and all these hammers would fly out there and they'd pick them up and start putting them back in there.

Well, this night Duke was in there. He wouldn't play nothing. He just listened and started writing things on his sleeves. He had tuxedo cuff sleeves and he was writing, writing little passages that he liked, and he was stealing like that, you see? And then next night would be like a trombone night. It was wonderful, a lot of fun.
To your knowledge, did any of those piano players ever recognize their material?
Oh, sure.
Did they ever say anything to Duke?

No, because they -- He was nothing. He couldn't join that bunch. That bunch was supposed to be the elite of the pianists and Duke was there to just listening. He was just like -- trying to steal -- some kid or something trying to learn something, which he was.
Do you know Mexico's real name?
No, I don't.
He came here, you know. He lived here for a while.

I know. He was in the Veterans Hospital here when I met him, although I didn't know -- When I met him I didn't know who he was. I just knew that there was somebody named Mexico in the fifties. When Duke would come
to town --
Uh-huh.

-- he would sign him out or get him signed out of the Veterans Hospital. I don't know whether he had TB or what but he had some affliction and was living in the hospital. But he would come out on a pass when Duke would come to town. And Duke was taking his life -- in fact, he had me working with him taking down his life story. I don't know whatever happened to the life story.
And later, after I didn't see Mexico anymore, I found out who Mexico was, and the only name I ever heard was just Mexico.
Uh-huh. That's all I knew, Mexico.
He was Mexican and Indian, I think, wasn't he?
Yeah, and Caloon.
(Laughter.)
I guess they're all mixed up.
And he said he grew up in a carnival. I remember him saying that, --
I wouldn't know.
-- traveling on the road as a child.
But they used to have a lot of fun there. Luis Russell had taught me a tune that was being popular around at that time, you know, and I wasn't known at all.

So one night they're going to have saxophone and clarinet nights. So Luis Russell says, "C'mon, I'm going to take you there." I said, "No, not me." He said, "Yes, you are, too." So I says, "Well, okay. Here goes." And I went in there and played a tune. You know, I could play pretty good, boy, and everybody was, "Oh, who's that character? Where did he come from?" Then I began to get known around there and that's how --
