Do you remember any of the other saxophonists or clarinetists who were playing there at the same time?
Oh, Buster Bailey, Procope, all them guys that were good clarinetists. They had one guy used to play in a theater. He was a West Indian. I can't think of his name. He was quite a musician, too.
How long was Mexico's open? How long did it last?

Oh, for years. I was there in '27 and when I left and went on the road with Duke there for quite a while, every time I'd come back to New York he still had his little spot there until the next thing you know he had disappeared.
And what was --
Then it got to be Minton's place.
Oh. Minton's was the same place that
Yeah, yeah.
Ah.
And it got to be his place. So evidently they must have did business, Minton and Mexico.

Minton was a nice guy because he used to be in the union, you know, a big shot. And at that time you couldn't work on a regular job in New York for six months when you first joined the union. But Minton, he'd let you go. He'd say, "Go ahead, son, go and meet" -- just don't worry -- because he had that part of the city to cover, you know, for musicians. He liked us. He gave all youngsters a break. Yeah, we got along all right.
That's where Duke used to lose all his money, at Minton's.
Gambling at Minton's?
Yeah.
When Minton's first opened, was there jam sessions and music like there was at -- ?
Yeah, yeah.
In the forties there were, but -- when did it open? In the thirties?
I guess so.
But Minton, he added gambling. You see, Mexico didn't have gambling, just drinking and music. But Minton, he
got that plus gambling, see.
Uh-huh.
So it was pretty good.
I think this is the end of this tape.
(End of Proceedings as recorded.)

During the period we were talking about in New York, it was somewhere around in there, was it not, that Sidney Bechet worked very briefly with Dukes Land this man?

Yeah, he worked -- See, Duke used to play a summer gig for a guy named Si Scribner in the New England states, and Sidney, he used to work with Duke -- Sidney -- and they'd go up there for about -- well, the Bubber summer months. Harry Carney and Bechet and Bubba and Braud.

And during that time, that period, Sidney was drinking heavy -- well, Sidney still drank heavy until he died. But one time he was telling us a story that they hadn't seen Sidney for two days and finally on the third night here comes Sidney. So Duke started to ask him, "Where have you been?" He said, "You won't believe this, but I was in a cab and fell asleep and I just woke up and here I am here." And everybody had to break up laughing because it was such a funny story, a lie.
(Laughing.)

And Bechet was funny because -- Paul Whiteman's group, they had heard about Bechet. So they were playing a dance at I think it was the Roseland and they all came over and Duke was playing, like, the intermission band, and all of Paul Whiteman's sax section came over there to hear. They wanted to hear Sidney Bechet.

So they told Sidney Bechet that Paul Whiteman's gang was in there to hear him. So they say what Sidney did was to take a handkerchief out of his pocket and put a part on his mouthpiece and the rest over his fingers so they couldn't see what he was fingering and what notes he was doing or nothing.
(Laughing.)

So then that broke up the place again, see. He was quite a guy. But they couldn't get along. And Sidney, bless his soul, and my teacher, Lorenzo Tio, they came to New York. Now, Lorenzo, he had just finished having a stroke, so he and Bechet got together and they were going to open up a speakeasy.

So they bought a lot of gin, bathtub gin they used to call it in those days, and the place -- they were going to paint the little one-horse room they had there for a bar. So that day they started painting and then they were looking, everybody couldn't find Bechet nor Tio. They didn't know where they were. They were looking for them. And both of those characters was drunk behind the bar.
(Laughter.)
They'd been drunk. They drank up all the booze that they were supposed to sell. So that was gone. But they did some awful things in those days.
So the reason that Bechet didn't spend any more time with Duke is because of his drinking? Is that

No. He could make more money without Duke. You see, Bechet wrote a lot of tunes, you know, and he would sell them just like we all did at the time. $25, $50. You know, it was kind of nice money for them to drink especially. Like I sold Mood Indigo for $25. That's, you know --
The other numbers that you mentioned that are in the discography, which I haven't had a chance to study yet, did you get paid for those? Did you sell those or were they -- ?
Yeah, I sold those but -- that's all -- but they put their name on it. They got all the money.
Did Bechet sell tunes to Duke, do you think?
Yeah, he sold tunes to Duke and Irving Mills and anybody.
Do you remember any of the tunes that Bechet wrote that --

I think one was, like, 'Honeysuckle Rose,' I think, something like that, but it's not 'Honeysuckle Rose.' It's something like it. It was from the show, from the Blackbird show. They put a couple of his number in that, but they got credit for it, not him. He was quite a guy, oh, boy.
In his book he says the reason that he couldn't stay with Duke was that he couldn't get along with
Charlie Irvis and Bubber Miley.
He can't get along with nobody. He's got a bad temper.
When Duke and the small unit would go up to New England in the summertime, what were you doing? That was during the period you were --
I wasn't there. I wasn't in New York at all.
Oh.

You see, I was -- that was after I joined Duke. And during the summer I used to go up in the New England states when he had the big band, see, and that's when he used to tell all the stories about Sidney and Bubber Miley and Otto Hardwick -- that's another one.
Why did Otto Hardwick leave the band?

I think he left by request. In other words, it's a funny thing, when I joined the band, Otto Hardwick, he wouldn't show up sometimes for two and three nights and I always wondered what is he doing. I knew he was a heavy drinker.

So one night I decided I'm going to hang out with him and find out what he's doing, you know. Then he called me, 'Let's go make bouzan.' I taught him how to say that -- bouzan. Let's go have a ball with drinking. He said, 'You going to make bouzan with me tonight?' I said, 'Yeah, I'm
with you." All he did was run from apartment to -- all of his friends, lady friends -- apartment to apartment, drinking and drinking until he got stoned. He got me so stoned I missed the night.
(Laughing.)
I says, "Oh, no." I couldn't believe it, but that's what he used to do and for no rhyme or reason. He'd just go out.

Herb Jeffries told in an interview the other day, I understand, a radio interviewer, that when he was with Duke, you and he used to go to restaurants, on the road, to get the food in places, I guess, in the south where they wouldn't serve colored people, --
Colored --

That's right. We came to St. Louis from a gig and so there wasn't a restaurant available to get something to eat. There was some, you know, but you couldn't go in there, see. So with the manager -- we had a little manager, Sam Flaschnik was his name -- and Herb and myself, whatever restaurant we'd see, we'd go up and we'd stop. So we saw this restaurant, there was nobody in it, the lights on. So Flaschnik said, "Watch, I'll fix that." He said, "Stop the bus back here and I'll go in front there." So he and Herb Jeffries and myself, we went into this restaurant and there's a guy coming out. It seemed as though he was so glad to see somebody in his place, see. So Sam said, "Can you serve 26 people right away?" So the guy says, "Depends on what they want." He said, "Well, ham and eggs, bacon and eggs." He says, "Oh, sure." He said, "I can fix it up as fast as you want it." He said, "Well, just fix up 26 right quick and I'll bring the people in because they're sitting out there." The guy says, "Sure." Sam says, "Now, when you're ready just holler."
So the guy, man, he fixed up those 26 plates and got it all fixed up, and Sam says, "Okay, fella,

bring them on in there. The stuff is ready." When they all walked in there and this guy saw it was nothing but coloons, he liked to have fainted. So Sam said, "What's the matter?" He said, "Uh, uh, nothing, nothing." But he wasn't going to throw that 26 -- those 26 plates away, though, you know. So we got to eating like that.

And so when we went into another place and just Sam and I went in there to get some sandwiches for the boys in the band, so Freddie Guy says, "Hell, if they can go in there, I can go in there too." you ran into it.

-- no troubles. Oh, we got smart. We had two Pullman's and a baggage car. So Duke found that out. So Duke come back there while we was cooking. He smelled that. You know, he liked to eat, you know. He said, "Oh, boy, that smells good." He said, "Where'd you guys get that?" We said, "We bought it. Where do you think we got it?" He said, "You got an extra one?" We said, "No." He said, "Can you get an extra one?" "Sure, we can get another one." He said, "How much?" So we got him like that. We made him buy the steaks or whatever we're going to do. "You buy it and we'll cook it and we'll give you some." So we got him like that, you see? Well, that paid for the stove and it paid for the gas, whatever. It paid for the food.

So I'm grabbing this girl by the arm and said, "C'mon, you got to go." She said, "I'm not going nowhere," and she was using all kind of vile language, you know. And I said, "Oh, we can't stand -- we can't have this in the house." And her purse was on this dresser. So I said, "Oh, yeah," and I'm pulling on her. You know, I'm starting to get rough with her? And I said, "Here. Take your purse and get on out of
here." And I picked up the purse and I feel a gun in there. You ought to see the big change.

"How long you want to stay in here?" I said, "Johnny shouldn't act that way with you. Where's that character?" I said, "Go get him." So Johnny said, "Put her out." I said, "You put her out. I know that later in your career you worked with Louig Armstrong. What about the difference in the music of Armstrong and Ellington?

Well, that's two different styles of music, to begin with. And Ellington has got a large band, Louie had a seven piece band, which -- and, to be truthful, I enjoyed both bands but I enjoyed Louig's more because I had more freedom in my playing, where Duke, you got to play what you see on the paper plus what you would say freedom, but it wasn't that much freedom. It doesn't give you a chance to even concentrate on really what you want to do because it's so short.
A set number of bars.
Yeah, that's what I'm saying. It comes within like eight bars, 16 bars, and that's it. But

with Armstrong you can play as many bars as you want because -- it doesn't bother you -- he doesn't bother you. The little band doesn't bother you. In other words, they tried to help you, to push you along, because they realized that they're small and every man counts. You know, it means something for each guy in the group where --
How was the spirit of the members of the band in Ellington compared with Armstrong's? The feelings of the men for the music and each other (unintelligible)?

Oh, I guess the feeling was all right. But I think that they were more close in Louis's aggregation because it's smaller, where Duke's is larger and they go like -- I hate to say that -- I mean, like cliques. Each band got cliques in the band. You know, like certain guys go with certain guys. But Armstrong's band's too small for that kind of business. You know what I mean.
Was there a competitive feeling in Duke's band among the men?
Oh, I don't think so. I mean, I think it could be a little jealousy feeling, that sometime -- but I don't think they thought about being competitive or nothing like that.
How about with Louis Armstrong?
No, you don't have time to think about anything like that with Louis. I mean, he was wonderful.
When I met you, you were with Louie and there was a five-piece band. Who were the other people? You said a seven-piece band.
Let's see. We had a drummer -- we had Cozy Cole at one time -- No, Big Sid, Teagarden. That's two. Who was playing piano? Oh, --
Earl was when I met you.

Yeah, but he wasn't -- I'm talking about the first band. Dick Carey played the piano. That's three. I played clarinet. That's four. And Arvell Shaw played bass. That's five. And, let's see, and Velma Middleton was six. She was the vocalist. That's about it, six.
(Unintelligible) when I met you.
Yeah, that's about it.
There was Earl and you and Jack Teagarden and Big Sid and Louie and Arvell and Velma.
Yeah, I didn't count Louie. Louie is seven; with the vocalist, that's six and Louie made it seven.
Louie and you and Earl, Arvell and Big Sid and Jack Teagarden.
Jack Teagarden.
Yeah, right, yeah. Okay.
Yeah.
But I enjoyed both of them. I know one thing, it's a wonderful experience. You couldn't buy it. To be known as
being one of the guys that played with two of the greatest. So what more can you ask for, huh?
In Louis's band there was no set structure. You could play a tune however you felt about it whenever you wanted?

You played the tune whenever you, how you -- whatever you felt and when and what tempo or anything and played as much as you want till you got tired, until you passed out if you wanted to. I mean, as long as it doesn't interfere with a schedule that they had, you know. I mean, like we'd go play dances or even concerts -- we'd play concerts -- Play as long as you want.
What kind of a person was Louis?
Louis was a wonderful man to work with. I mean, he'd say a lot of things. He can raise hell with you. Now in two seconds he'd forgotten all about it and forgot even what it was all about.

I kidded him. One time, for no reason whatsoever -- we were at the Blue Note in Chicago -- and, well, if he had a fuss with his wife, Lucille, and he came off the stand. He said, 'Cats think because they played in a big band that they are the best musicians in town, the greatest band. They think they're hell and everyone thinks because he was with Paul Whiteman, he thinks he's hell, too.' So I'm listening. I said, 'What is all this about?'

And I hadn't even said one word to him. Neither has Jack. Nobody. And he's mumbling all this in his dressing room. So I said, "Well, I know you must be hinting at me, but if you are, I'm sure glad I was with the greatest band in the world, because your band wasn't nothing." I said, "You had the world's worst band." And he kept griping.
(Laughter.)
(Laughter.)
Oh, boy. That's the truth. He had good men in his band but they didn't have no good arrangements, nothing. I was surprised. If it wasn't for him, there wouldn't be any band.
And you're talking about a man that can remember tunes of the past years and people of the past years. He had that memory. He was phenomenal. I've never seen anybody like that.

Another guy like that is Sonny Greer if he's straight. He could remember, because people used to come in the Cotton Club all the time and talk to Duke and Duke would say, "Who's that, Sonny?" And he say, "Don't you remember him? That's so and so from so and so." He said, "Oh, yeah."

I got to tell you this good one about Duke. You know, Duke, he's contrary at times, you know, like people would come in and ask him to play a tune and he'll give you that grin, "Yeah. Okay, yeah." So this is at the Cotton Club and this gangster had did time for one of the big bosses there.

And, oh, he's a big rugged Irishman. Bad, real bad. So he came in there and the day they brought him to the Cotton Club they'd got him a big Lincoln limousine, bought him that, gave him money, and got him a little beautiful blond gal. So he came in there -- so he dances like them old Bowery boys, you know. He can't hardly do nothing he's so stiff. You know, and stiff in everything. So he gets around to the piano and said, "Hey, fella, will you play 'Singing in the Rain?'" The Duke, "Yeah, Just's "Singing in the Rain."

Another set come on, no 'Singing in the Rain.' The third set come on, he comes around there and he grabbed Duke by the neck. "I asked you to play 'Singing in the Rain,' God damn it." And so Herman Stark, the manager, had to run up and grab this guy and talk to him and talk him away from Duke. And Herman Stark came back and said, "Duke, are you crazy?" Duke said, "What do you mean crazy?" He said, "He asked me for 'Singing in the Rain.' I'm going to play it." He said, "Yeah, you're going to play it when?" He said, "Pretty soon, yeah." He said, "Do you know that guy?" He said, "He just did a stretch for Frenchie from killing -- " Duke said, "Huh?" "From killing -- Yeah, yeah, [he's] killing." "He did?" We played "Singing in the Rain" for an hour.
(Laughter.)
Honest to God, we played -- Oh, boy, there was some -- and from then on, when they was hotfooting,

all these big guys, you know, like, Rudy Vallee when he was in his prime and all that, this guy was Duke's bodyguard. He'd go get Duke from the theater with his machine gun between his legs, and they had a bulletproof glass.
Whom did Duke need protection from?
The rest of the gangsters. The other gangsters didn't know anything about it.

You see, there was two factions. The big one in New York was Owhrey Madden and he's -- and the other one was Capone. They was just like that, you know, so they had to protect their men from each other. And, brother, that was something. And poor Duke, he used to be so glad when that man would bring him back. I said, "That's what you get for being so smart."
I think in the Ulann book Duke tells the story of having played a request for Legs Diamond and getting a thousand dollar tip.

He might have. I don't know that part. But I know that one, though. I'm trying to think of his name and I know it real well, and he had -- boy, but Duke, every time the man, anything he wanted; if Duke was playing the "Rachachacha," he'd stop and play it, what he wanted.

Oh.

-- on the trombone?
Right.
Tom, a bass player, and Edward, the bass drum.
Yeah, I guess so, but I didn't know the
drummer and the other one. I knew Vic and Octave. They were the most important ones to know because they got the work.
Uh-huh.
And when we first talked about King Oliver, at the time you joined him there were two band members whose name but you couldn't remember them.
George Fields was one, the trombonist.
Uh-huh.
And --
The trumpet player?
The trumpet player was Bob Schaffner.
Is it true -- Excuse me.
Sure.
Were you talking about Schaffner?
Schaffner.
You have something else you were going to say about Schaffner?
Yeah, I was going to say he was quite a musician, that guy. . He was -- I think he was originally from St. Louis and he migrated to Chicago, then he lived in Chicago.
How long was he with King Oliver, do you know?
Oh, quite a few -- couple of -- three years, I imagine.
Well, he didn't go on to New York,

with King Oliver, did he?
obviously

No, he didn't go on to New York with us. That's when he -- he had lip trouble and he had to have it pierced and he knew only about one doctor in St. Louis that could do the job. And after he had it pierced, then he couldn't play for quite a while till it healed properly.
I think in Stanley Dance's book he mentions that you said that King Oliver was having problems, too.

Well, King Oliver, he had pyorrhea real bad, and in those days, I mean, they didn't treat pyorrhea like they do now, you know. A lot of times the poor man was suffering so bad he couldn't even blow his horn and his teeth would hit the roof of his mouth half of the time, they were so weak.
Is it true that King Oliver originated the mute for trumpet?
Yes.
With a bottle? is That right Do you know?

No, with his hand. He did all those things with his hand, and this fellow Harmon, Paddy Harmon, he sent -- he had a big ballroom and lots of money -- and he sent some guy to watch him to see how he was doing it. Then he invented a mute that he could make a similar noise but not exactly the same but real close.
Uh-huh.
And they used to call it the "qua-qua" mute, and he made a lot of money off it. He got wealthy. He got more rich. And that's it.
Then King Oliver didn't ever profit from it?
No.
It was his idea.
No, but he could do most anything with his hand without a mute. He never used a mute.

You mentioned a comedy team who were performing when Rocking in Rhythm was put together by members of the band. You said the comedy team was Johnny Lee and you couldn't remember his partner's name. Did you think of his partner's name?

No, I couldn't think -- I still can't think of it, but I know it was Johnny Lee and somebody else, and they used to sing that little parody. What they had, "But I got the number" and "Where did you get it from." "Big John told me," and it keeps going like that. They were just patting their feet and saying these things.

So we go on the stage and we sat there and finally, between Hodges and myself, we thought up this little ditty, (humming), and first thing you know, Duke got on to it and he made a tune and called it "Rocking in Rhythm." So we didn't get a dime out of it anyway. So then the latest thing, when it
came out, he had Harry Carney (had) wrote "Rocking in Rhythm," composed it. Harry never composed nothing in his life. So that was funny.
Do you suppose he put Harry's name on it --
Yeah, he did.
(just) to upset you and Johnny?
No. He couldn't upset me.

I have here the copy of Clarinet Gumbo, your new record on RCA, and I was wondering about the liner notes which are not signed, but for one thing, it says, one line is, "Despite his father being a violinist" -- speaking about you --
Yeah.

-- "and his family's hope that he would pursue a musical career, Barney at first was not too sure what he really wanted in life. It seems a certain amount of parental pressure was needed to spur the young man on. He studied clarinet with the legendary Lorenzo Tio. Tio had also taught Nicholas and Bechet."
Well, you've mentioned that you studied with Tio, but your father was not a violinist.
No, my father was no musician at all. It was my uncle.
Your uncle Emile that we talked about.
And in the next paragraph, it says, "As required of most reed men Bigard also doubled on sax, eventually joining a group Albert Nicholas headed at Tom Anderson's in New Orleans."
That's right.
Is that right?
That's right.
Because you hadn't mentioned Tom Anderson.

Also on these liner notes, Barney, it says, "Probably the best known of Bigard's own contributions to the monumental Ellington book of originals is the sultry Mood Indigo, originally titled "Dreamy Blues.""
Is that right? We didn't -- "Dreamy Blues?"
Not as I know of.
I never read that title before.
No.
The now classic clarinet-trombone There were other Bigard contributions, such as "Rocking in Rhythm," "Stompy Jones," "Saturday Night Function," and "C Jam Blues."
Well, --
What about --
-- some of it is wrong.
What is wrong?
"C Jam" is wrong to begin with.
Stompy Jones is okay. What's that other one you --
"Saturday Night Function" and Rocking in Rhythm which we --
Yeah, "Saturday Night Function" is right.
But I think Rex Stewart also mentions -- credits "C Jam" Blues to you but he says you said that you wrote it, that you --
No, I didn't tell Rex. He's day-dreaming.
Who wrote "C Jam" Blues? Do you know?
"C Jam" Blues? Duke, I think. I don't know.

In his chapter, "Illustrious Barney Bigard," in Rex's book Jazz Masters of the Thirties, Rex says, "In addition to joining in the jollity, Barney also was inspired to create melodies during those Ellington days. Among the credits he claims are "Mood Indigo," "Saratoga Swing," "Minuet in Blue," "Saturday Night Function," "Stompy Jones," "Clouds in My Heart," "Rocking in Rhythm." There are many others, too, that he sold or gave away."
So I guess he doesn't say "C Jam". I beg your pardon.
But I have read someplace else in some of the material --
Uh-huh.
-- that somebody else said that you wrote "C-Jam."
Yeah, but they were wrong. They even believed it, all in Europe, that I wrote that. So I just let them think it.
It was first called C Blues, right? And you recorded it with your small unit, didn't you?
Yes, I recorded it first and then they got the big band together, I guess, and -- [LONG PAUSE]

In the home of Barney and Dorothee Bigard there are some very interesting awards, trophies, plaques, showing some marvelous honors for a long career, and Mrs. Dorothee Bigard has made a list of all of them. We haven't really had a chance to discuss all of them, so I'm going to give the microphone to Mrs. Bigard right now and she and Barney will talk.

Thank you, Pat. Oh, I just wanted to be sure that a note was made on Barney's achievements which are well deserved and should be recognized, and that he was listed in Who's Who in America and has been since 1949, and his -- At the New Orleans Jazzfest in 1972, he was given the key to the city by the mayor of New Orleans, Mayor Landrieu, and also Achievement of Merit -- Merit of Achievement, rather, a plaque which is a beautiful honor for

Barney and well deserved. And he also has received an award for the Hall of Fame from the National Academy of Recording Artists and Sciences for being the songwriter, namely Barney Bigard, of 'Mood Indigo.' [and Grammy Award].
Would you like to say something about that, Honey?
Yeah.
That merit thing from New Orleans was really a gasser, --
The key.

-- especially that key. You know, that key is so large. It's about as big as a gnat's ass, and I enjoyed it, so I got it -- it's a specialty in my den. And I like for everybody that comes around and visits me to see it. I make it a point that they see that key, it's such a beauty. But all in all it's really beautiful. I like it very much. I enjoyed every bit of it. And then, the rest of it, why, --
In France.
-- and last year when I was in France, they made a shot of my -- what was it?
It was done by J. C. Averty.
J. C. Averty. He's a director of a studio, of my --
Excuse me. 'A Musical Biography of Barney Bigard' for French television. And we haven't heard
whether it's been shown over there yet -- Or not.
-- or not. But it was really a fantastic thing.

Yeah. And it was a hot day that day, so they had to bring us some spirits to keep us going and which we -- it was pretty nice, and it should come out all right. But you know the Frenchmen, it takes them so long to do anything. I mean, it may come out in three years, four years, five years. Who knows? But it was worth it. I enjoyed doing it.
And also you received last year at the Newport Jazz Festival George Welin's Hall of Fame award.
Yeah, that was nice. That was very nice.
His first Hall of Fame award which was really a great honor to be one of 11 musicians out of all the thousands of musicians in America. It was indeed a great honor and it was a fantastic concert.

Yes, it was. It was a beautiful concert and I enjoyed it very much. And I wanted to thank George Welk. He says, 'Well, you don't have to thank me because you deserve every bit of it. You should have had it years ago.' I said, 'Well, I don't know about that. I was too young to have it years ago.' And he laughed and we all laughed. But it was
really nice and it was enjoyable.

I think that covers everything.
Only, there's one thing. They gave me a disc in Nice, France, and it's all in Latin and I can't read Latin, so -- but I'm looking for some kind of a thing where I could put it, encase it in something that it would stand up and put it on one of the shelves in my den. It's a beautiful --
It was given to him by the mayor of Nice.
Yeah, it was given by the mayor of Nice, and with the help of the mayor of New Orleans --
And, incidentally, the mayor of Nice has all your records.
Yes, and he's a jazz fan and he always did like me and he liked my work and he congratulated me, and I met his gorgeous wife, as we all know her --
And Princess Grace.

Princess Grace. So it was nice.
So I think that about covers everything around and it's been real great.
Did you mention the Esquire awards?
And --
Oh, no. The Esquire awards.
I got -- Well, I have three Esquire awards when they were giving them out.
Silver.
Silver. I got the silver one. Benny Goodman got the gold. And that was for three years straight. So that was nice, too.
It's a nice collection --
So I can't complain and I enjoyed every bit of it. I'm trying to get some more and I'm working at it, and see how long I can last.
You have a long ways to go, my love.
(End of Proceedings as recorded.)

segments.title: Copyright notice, Smithsonian header and opening of reel one
segments.summary: Copyright notice, transcription header, and Willard opening the April 1976 interview.

segments.title: Name, birth date and the family house on Villere Street
segments.summary: Willard checks his name and birth date against published sources; he was born March 3, 1906 at 1726 Villere Street in the seventh ward, lived there all his life, and the house was sold cheaply at auction after his grandmother died.

segments.title: First kids' band playing 'The Sheik' for gate money
segments.summary: He left for Chicago at 18; before that he and boyhood friends such as Landry learned together, knew three tunes including 'The Sheik', and played yard parties for a quarter apiece.

segments.title: First big band with Gaspard and the 'Tiger Rag' rehearsal
segments.summary: A neighbour named Gaspard needed a clarinetist, persuaded Bigard's family to let him play, and the first piece at rehearsal was 'Tiger Rag'; Bigard, reading straight four-four, could not get the dance two-four feel.

segments.title: Moving from clarinet to tenor and soprano saxophone
segments.summary: Clarinet was his main instrument but he thought he was awful, so when saxophone came out he played tenor and soprano and put the clarinet down, which is how he went to Chicago.

segments.title: King Oliver buys him a clarinet and he returns to it
segments.summary: With Oliver he played tenor and soprano beside clarinetists Albert Nicholas and Darnell Howard; when they left for China Oliver bought him a new Conn clarinet and he took up clarinet again for good.

segments.title: Milwaukee with Charlie Elgar and Omer Simeon
segments.summary: After Oliver he went to Milwaukee with Charlie Elgar's band, where Omer Simeon, a fine clarinetist who never got his due, helped him and he blossomed.

segments.title: Leaving Oliver, New York, and the Savoy band battle
segments.summary: He dates leaving Oliver to about 1925; in New York the band battled Chick Webb and Fletcher Henderson at the Savoy but Oliver would not take the money offered, leaving them without a job.

segments.title: Banjoist Willie Santiago and the fish in the sun
segments.summary: A story of Willie Santiago, who slept through jobs, and the night he was to cook for the club, bought a red snapper, got drunk and fell asleep under a tree with the fish in the sun.

segments.title: Luis Russell's band at the Nest Club and the Broadway tips
segments.summary: He joined Luis Russell at the Nest Club, working ten to six or seven in the morning for Broadway stars like Helen Morgan and Harry Richman; salary was $84 a week with tips almost as much.

segments.title: Misunderstanding the boss's 'get off' at the Nest
segments.summary: Not knowing New York lingo, Bigard thought 'get off' meant leave the stand and began packing his horn; the boss meant he should take a chorus, and the band teased him.

segments.title: Wellman Braud brings him to Duke Ellington's Cotton Club band
segments.summary: Wellman Braud recommended him to Ellington, who was starting at the Cotton Club for about $72 a week; the Nest boss offered his job back if it failed, and Bigard joined Duke in late 1927.

segments.title: How early New Orleans bands worked without readers
segments.summary: Bigard says critics misunderstand Dixieland: bands had a violinist leader because few horn players could read, so others fingered their own parts by ear since whites would not teach Black players.

segments.title: Lorenzo Tio and Papa Tio as clarinet teachers
segments.summary: Few Black music teachers existed; Bigard's own teacher was Lorenzo Tio, whose uncle Papa Tio bluntly turned away pupils without talent and took a liking to Bigard.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet could not read music
segments.summary: Bechet, as great as he was, could not read music; Bigard did not know him in New Orleans but met him later in New York.

segments.title: Playing around New Orleans before Chicago and the 'Slap Tongue King'
segments.summary: He was only starting in the New Orleans scene when he left for Oliver; he worked with Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly, Manuel Perez and Piron, learned from Amos White, and was known as the Slap Tongue King until broken reeds cost too much.

segments.title: Learning to read from his uncle and starting on Dodds's E-flat clarinet
segments.summary: His fiddle-playing uncle taught him to read music; Johnny Dodds lent him a small E-flat clarinet because his fingers were too small, and at 14 he bought his own B-flat clarinet.

segments.title: End of reel one and start of reel two
segments.summary: Reel one ends mid-sentence and the reel two header and proceedings begin.

segments.title: Subbing for Big Eye Louie Nelson at Lake Pontchartrain picnics
segments.summary: Subbing at lake picnics for Big Eye Louie Nelson, Bigard was teased by Zutty Singleton as a snake charmer, held one wrong note, and was comforted by banjoist Willie Bontemps.

segments.title: Playing all-day parades in New Orleans for 75 cents
segments.summary: Parades for unions and clubs ran from nine to five for 75 cents; he began at 14 or 15, proud of his hat and blue shirt, and remembers sore feet.

segments.title: Funerals, tombs and the second line
segments.summary: Describes playing sad music to the vault, then 'Didn't He Ramble' and the second line afterward, including Crip, who led on his peg leg.

segments.title: Working as a cigar maker and photo engraver as a boy
segments.summary: Before music he worked at 11 or 12 for his uncle in cigars, disliked the conditions, then at 13 or 14 worked for the Russian photo engraver Romansky making prints for the Sunday paper.

segments.title: Wanting to play trumpet but being steered to clarinet
segments.summary: He wanted trumpet but his family said he lacked wind and, since he whistled well, urged clarinet; he later felt too far gone on clarinet to switch.

segments.chapter: King Oliver's band and early jazz
segments.title: Tom Anderson's, Albert Nicholas leaving, and the call from Oliver
segments.summary: Oliver had not known him; Bigard was laid off at Tom Anderson's when Albert Nicholas quietly left for Chicago, the boss begged him back with a $10 raise to $35, and Luis Russell later had Joe send for him.

segments.chapter: King Oliver's band and early jazz
segments.title: Who was in King Oliver's band when he joined
segments.summary: He lists Albert Nicholas, Darnell Howard, Paul Barbarin, Luis Russell, Bert Cobb and Bud Scott, but cannot recall a trombonist and another trumpeter.

segments.chapter: King Oliver's band and early jazz
segments.title: The word 'jazz' and not knowing Scott Joplin was Black
segments.summary: The word was spelled many ways and the music was called hot music or jazz; his uncle ordered Scott Joplin band sets and Bigard assumed Joplin was white.

segments.chapter: King Oliver's band and early jazz
segments.title: Black composers of the day and Jelly Roll Morton's claim on 'St. Louis Blues'
segments.summary: The only Black composers he knew were Piron and Clarence Williams; he thinks Jelly Roll wrote 'St. Louis Blues' and recounts how Jelly Roll got advances from Melrose by writing tunes.

segments.title: Copyrighting his own tunes with Paul Barbarin
segments.summary: He copyrighted tunes with Paul Barbarin by mailing them to Washington, but does not know what became of them.

segments.title: How 'Rocking in Rhythm' came about and Harry Carney's credit
segments.summary: Bigard says Duke put Carney's name on 'Rocking in Rhythm' though Carney wrote nothing; the theme grew from his own humming and Braud and Carney joining behind two comedians in Baltimore, and Duke made the arrangement.

segments.title: Duke Ellington taking credit: Sophisticated Lady
segments.summary: Lawrence Brown and Otto Hardwick fooled with the tune in a dressing room and Duke turned it into 'Sophisticated Lady'; Bigard says Duke did not credit his men though he did compose good numbers.

segments.title: Writing 'Mood Indigo'
segments.summary: Bigard says Duke wrote the first part and he wrote the other part; it was recorded with his small group, Mills took it, he got $25, and his name came onto it through ASCAP only after 28 years.

segments.title: Barney's small group out of the Ellington band
segments.summary: The recording group was billed under Bigard's name; he remembers Whetsol, Tricky Sam, Duke and Sonny, and a second group with Tizol, Ben Webster and Rex Stewart.

segments.title: Composing 'Lament for Javanette' at the Sherman Hotel
segments.summary: He made up the tune alone on the bandstand in Chicago while girls dressed as Javanese sold cigarettes; Duke added an introduction and put his name on it.

segments.title: Ellington's first band and why Europe wants the old records
segments.summary: Duke took ideas from his players' solos; Bigard says he never had a band like his first one and audiences in Europe want the old records, not the newer music.

segments.title: End of reel two and start of reel three, June 1976
segments.summary: Bigard asks how many hours they have gone, reel two ends, and Willard opens reel three on June 23, 1976.

segments.title: Follow-up: Landry, the three-tune band, and Gaspard's name
segments.summary: Henry Landry was the trumpeter in the kids' band that played two sheiks and the blues for gate receipts; Bigard cannot yet recall Gaspard's full name.

segments.title: The China trip: Albert Nicholas, Darnell Howard and Teddy Weatherford
segments.summary: A Chicago drummer took a big group to China; Nicholas and Howard went, stayed two years at a big hotel, and returned broke, as did Weatherford who stayed on.

segments.title: Uncles Emile and Ulysses Bigard
segments.summary: The fiddle-playing uncle was Emile Bigard and another uncle, the cigar maker, was Ulysses Bigard.

segments.title: Pronouncing Bigard and Villere; Creole and American New Orleans
segments.summary: He explains the American versus patois pronunciations and that Canal Street divided the American section from the French-speaking Creole section, who rarely mixed.

segments.title: French spoken at home and his grandmother's French books
segments.summary: He speaks some French, his family spoke only French and attended an all-French school, and he shows his grandmother's old French books.

segments.title: Grandparents, parents and who raised him
segments.summary: His grandfather Emile came from Lille, France; his mother Emmanuela died at his birth and his grandmother Eugenia raised him with uncles and a brother.

segments.title: His brothers Alec and Sidney
segments.summary: Brother Alec is a drummer who can no longer hear; Bigard could not play with him; brother Sidney was shot in a fight over his wife.

segments.title: Buddy Petit, the stuttering trumpeter, arrested for his contracts
segments.summary: Buddy Petit took deposits on many jobs; at a longshoremen's picnic a cop doubted he was Petit, and when Petit produced a pile of contracts as proof he was taken to jail.

segments.title: Uncle teaches him to read; Johnny Dodds lends an E-flat clarinet
segments.summary: His uncle taught him to read music and divide bars, not fingering; Dodds, who played in the uncle's band, lent a little E-flat clarinet that small fingers could manage.

segments.title: Lessons with Lorenzo Tio, reluctantly arranged by his uncle
segments.summary: Lorenzo Tio, who played with Piron's society band, began teaching him; Lorenzo begged his old uncle to take Bigard on, and the old man liked him and taught him the rest of the way.

segments.title: Tio's symphony band and getting fired as a snake charmer
segments.summary: Tio asked what music he wanted to play; Bigard said jazz, though playing in Tio's club symphony band helped his reading, and at a club job near Oswego the boss fired him for holding one note.

segments.title: From soprano and tenor back to clarinet for good
segments.summary: Retells that he took up the new soprano and tenor saxophones, then returned to clarinet when Oliver bought him one, and now never plays saxophone.

segments.title: The 'snake charmer' nickname and learning slap tongue
segments.summary: The snake charmer name lasted as long as he was in New Orleans; he learned slap tongue from Louie Warnecke in Piron's band, became the King of the Slap Tongue and took revenge by not showing up for jobs.

segments.title: Wellman Braud, who called him 'Millet'
segments.summary: Millet is a New Orleans nickname used between him and Braud, who became his best friend and guided him in New York and in Duke's band.

segments.title: Back to New Orleans: parade pay and the trumpeter who passed for white
segments.summary: He repeats the 75-cent parade story and tries without success to recall the name of the light-skinned trumpet player who would not teach Black pupils.

segments.title: Duke's apartment, Edna's razor scar, and where the Nest was
segments.summary: Visiting Duke's apartment on Seventh Avenue, Bigard recalls that Duke's wife Edna had cut his face; the Nest was an after-hours joint around the corner from Connie's Inn.

segments.title: Nest after-hours tips versus the Ellington job
segments.summary: At the Nest he made $40 or $50 in tips over his $75 pay but left for Duke, and Braud's encouragement that the band would go places kept him there.

segments.title: Edna and Mildred Dixon, Duke's wives and partners
segments.summary: Bigard knew little of Edna, whom he calls evil, and likes Mildred Dixon, who danced at the Cotton Club with Henry Wesson; he will not name who caused Edna to slit Duke's face.

segments.title: Mildred saves Duke's finances; Bea and Willie Bryant
segments.summary: Mildred gave Duke her salary to pay the band when he gambled and he treated her badly; when the Cotton Club moved to Broadway he took up with Bea, who had been with Willie Bryant and Joe Louis.

segments.title: Duke's bodyguards Weak Knees and Jonesy
segments.summary: Bigard calls Duke a coward who had a Washington bodyguard called Weak Knees and a valet, Jonesy, and once tricked Bigard into breakfast as his protection.

segments.title: The time Bigard nearly beat Duke
segments.summary: Duke interfered in Bigard's love life; Bigard grabbed him by the neck before Cootie caught his arm, and he thinks Tizol once wanted to cut Duke.

segments.title: Duke sent no flowers when Bigard's father died
segments.summary: Duke collected money for flowers for friends' deaths but said nothing when Bigard's father died, which Bigard never forgave.

segments.title: About thirteen tunes without credit, including 'Rocking in Rhythm'
segments.summary: He says he has about thirteen uncredited tunes in the discography, including 'Saturday Night Function', and that Duke put Carney's name on 'Rocking in Rhythm' though Carney could not compose.

segments.title: Harry Carney's devotion and Duke's family
segments.summary: Willard says Carney treated Duke like a father; Bigard says Duke treated his own son badly, favoured his sister Ruth, and adored his mother.

segments.title: Duke's aversion to the color brown
segments.summary: Willard asks if Duke's dislike of brown came from his mother's death; Bigard never heard that and says Duke did not trust him or fool with him.

segments.title: Where Duke's nickname 'Dumpy' came from
segments.summary: Bigard thinks the name came from Freddie Guy and Sonny Greer and says Duke disliked being called it.

segments.title: Duke never fired anyone, he made them quit
segments.summary: Bigard says Duke made people so miserable they quit; he could not do it to Bubber Miley or Otto Hardwick, hounded Freddie Guy out, and eventually fired Sonny Greer.

segments.title: Ellington's drummers after Sonny Greer and Louie Bellson
segments.summary: They list the drummers after Sonny, from Bellson to Sam Woodyard; Bigard says most could not cut the mustard and Bellson was good but his marriage to Pearl Bailey ended it.

segments.title: Duke's late-life decline and rehearsing at the 1973 Carnegie concert
segments.summary: Bigard thinks Duke grew senile rather than paranoid; for George Wein's Carnegie Hall reunion he rehearsed 'Rose Room' with Duke, and Ray Nance told him of a threat from Duke's valet.

segments.title: Duke's snubs of Sonny Greer and Ray Nance on the concert night
segments.summary: Duke brushed off Sonny Greer, introduced Bigard briefly and played the tune too slowly, and never called Ray Nance from the wings.

segments.title: More of Duke's late cruelties: Norris Turney and Tony Watkins
segments.summary: Willard tells how Duke doubled the tempo behind Norris Turney until he quit and left Tony Watkins waiting in the wings of a television show; Bigard agrees he got terrible.

segments.title: Mexico's speakeasy cutting contests with Duke jotting on his cuffs
segments.summary: Mexico's basement joint near the Lafayette Theater held piano nights with James P. Johnson, Willie the Lion and Fats Waller, and Duke only listened and wrote passages on his shirt cuffs.

segments.title: Who Mexico was: his real name and the Veterans Hospital
segments.summary: Neither knows Mexico's real name; Willard met him in a Los Angeles Veterans Hospital where Duke arranged for him to go out on pass and had her taking down his life story.

segments.title: Bigard's first sax and clarinet night at Mexico's
segments.summary: Luis Russell pushed him to play at Mexico's clarinet night, where his playing made him known, and other clarinetists there were Buster Bailey and Procope.

segments.title: Mexico's becomes Minton's with gambling
segments.summary: Mexico's lasted for years until it became Minton's place; Minton, a union official, let young musicians work, and he added gambling where Duke lost his money.

segments.title: End of reel three and start of reel four
segments.summary: Willard notes the tape is ending and the reel four header begins.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet's summers with Duke and his cab story
segments.summary: Duke played summer gigs in New England for Si Scribner with Bechet, Carney and Braud, and Bechet explained two days missing by claiming he fell asleep in a cab.

segments.title: Bechet covers his fingers from Paul Whiteman's saxophones
segments.summary: When Whiteman's saxophone section came to hear Bechet at Roseland, he draped a handkerchief over his mouthpiece and hands so they could not see his fingering.

segments.title: Lorenzo Tio and Bechet drink their own speakeasy's gin
segments.summary: Tio, after a stroke, and Bechet planned a speakeasy in New York and were found drunk behind the bar having drunk all the stock.

segments.title: Bechet selling tunes and why he left Duke
segments.summary: Bechet could earn more without Duke and, like Bigard, sold tunes for $25 or $50, some to Duke and Irving Mills; Bigard says Bechet could not get along with anybody.

segments.title: Otto Hardwick's disappearances and 'making bouzan'
segments.summary: Otto Hardwick often missed nights; when Bigard went along, Hardwick ran from apartment to apartment drinking until Bigard missed the job.

segments.title: First European trip with Ellington in 1933
segments.summary: Europe with Duke in 1933 or 1934 was a thrill; they played only two shows at the London Palladium and ducked the crowds at the stage door.

segments.title: Missing this summer's European tour after his operation
segments.summary: He missed two European dates this year after his operation, including the Nice festival with George Wein, and Benny Carter went in his place.

segments.title: Crossing the Atlantic with Ellington: Braud's storm and toupee
segments.summary: He likes sea travel; Braud blamed Bigard for talking up a storm when the ship showed a movie called Storm at Daybreak, and later threw his London toupee into the ocean.

segments.chapter: Jump for Joy and the Harlem clubs
segments.title: Jump for Joy gets fixed in Los Angeles
segments.summary: The Ellington show 'Jump for Joy' broke in Los Angeles, Nick Castle choreographed, and a movie actor Bigard cannot name fixed the slow parts so houses packed; backers pulled out, Duke was too scared to carry it himself, and it closed despite good tunes.

segments.chapter: Jump for Joy and the Harlem clubs
segments.title: Cotton Club, Connie's Inn and Small's Paradise shows
segments.summary: Cotton Club shows were good when stars like Ethel Waters or Peg Leg Bates appeared; Connie's Inn, run by gangsters, and Small's Paradise also had good shows.

segments.chapter: Ellington band members and life on the road
segments.title: Mistaking Benny Waters for Benny Carter at Charlie Johnson's
segments.summary: Sitting in with Charlie Johnson's band, Bigard took Benny Waters for Benny Carter, judged him unimpressive, then met the real Carter, who was arranging in the back, and was embarrassed.

segments.chapter: Ellington band members and life on the road
segments.title: Who joined Ellington before and after Bigard, and Elmer Snowden
segments.summary: Harry Carney was in the band before Bigard; Hodges, Cootie, Tizol and Whetsol came after, and the Washington men pushed banjoist Elmer Snowden out and made Duke leader.

segments.chapter: Ellington band members and life on the road
segments.title: Finding food in segregated towns with Herb Jeffries and Sam Flaschnik
segments.summary: On tour the band could not eat in many restaurants, so manager Sam Flaschnik, Jeffries and Bigard tricked a St. Louis cafe into cooking 26 meals, and Freddie Guy was told to use the back door even as a Creole.

segments.chapter: Ellington band members and life on the road
segments.title: Cooking steaks in the baggage car and making Duke pay
segments.summary: Living on the band's Pullman cars, Bigard and Billy Taylor cooked on a kerosene stove and soon had Duke buying the steaks while they cooked them.

segments.chapter: Ellington band members and life on the road
segments.title: Johnny Hodges, chicken and his straight face
segments.summary: Bigard and Willard recall Hodges cooking and eating chicken and corn on the cob, and how his straight face hid his humor.

segments.chapter: Ellington band members and life on the road
segments.title: Hodges, the girl in Washington, and the gun in her purse
segments.summary: Hodges got Bigard to throw out a tough girlfriend at a Washington boarding house until Bigard found a gun in her purse.

segments.title: Playing with Armstrong versus Ellington: freedom and cliques
segments.summary: Bigard preferred Armstrong's small band because he could play as many bars as he wished, while Duke's big band confined solos to eight or sixteen bars and had cliques.

segments.title: The members of Armstrong's All-Stars
segments.summary: He lists Cozy Cole or Big Sid Catlett, Jack Teagarden, Dick Carey or Earl Hines, Arvell Shaw and Velma Middleton, and values having played with two of the greatest.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong as a bandleader and the Blue Note outburst
segments.summary: With Louis you could play as long as you wanted; he blew up fast and forgot, and at the Blue Note in Chicago after a fight with Lucille he griped about big-band men until Bigard answered that Whiteman's band was the worst.

segments.title: Duke's and Sonny Greer's memory for faces and tunes
segments.summary: Bigard says Duke had a phenomenal memory and so could Sonny Greer, who would remind him who visitors at the Cotton Club were.

segments.title: The gangster who wanted 'Singing in the Rain' at the Cotton Club
segments.summary: A newly released gangster asked Duke for 'Singing in the Rain', Duke put him off, and after the manager Herman Stark explained who the man was the band played it for an hour.

segments.title: The gangster as Duke's bodyguard and rival mobs
segments.summary: The gangster became Duke's bodyguard with a machine gun and bulletproof glass because of rival factions of Owney Madden and Capone; Willard mentions a Legs Diamond tip.

segments.title: First meeting and hearing Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: He first met Armstrong in Chicago after Louis had left Oliver, and in New Orleans they knew his records, with 'Cornet Chop Suey' and Bechet's 'Wildcat Blues' heard on every street.

segments.title: From the film 'New Orleans' to Louis Armstrong's All-Stars
segments.summary: Working with Armstrong in Hollywood for the film 'New Orleans' with Zutty, Kid Ory, Bud Scott and Red Callender led to a trial at Billy Berg's, then a road tour, and the All-Stars name.

segments.chapter: Leaving Duke and the Hollywood years
segments.title: Why he left Ellington in 1942
segments.summary: Wartime train travel meant sitting in the aisle, he met the woman who became his wife in Los Angeles and stayed, having lost admiration for Duke after the incident about his father; they remained friendly.

segments.chapter: Leaving Duke and the Hollywood years
segments.title: Freelancing, Billy Berg's and touring with Freddie Slack
segments.summary: After Duke he led his own groups, played Billy Berg's and studio work, and for two years traveled with Freddie Slack, making almost a movie a month, including some with Fred Astaire.

segments.chapter: Leaving Duke and the Hollywood years
segments.title: Earning more after Duke, and the raise he won in 1930
segments.summary: He made more money after leaving Duke and most with Louie, whose overhead was smaller, while Duke and Irving Mills kept the money and refused raises; he once quit in New York to get one.

segments.title: End of reel four and start of reel five, June 30, 1976
segments.summary: The tape ends and reel five begins on June 30, 1976, continuing the interview.

segments.title: Duke composing the Cotton Club show on the spot and Calloway's lost bet
segments.summary: Duke never wrote introductions or endings down; he gave each man his notes and rhythm at rehearsal, and Cab Calloway lost a bet with Herman Stark that the show would not open on time.

segments.title: Duke's claim about writing 'Mood Indigo' at breakfast
segments.summary: Bigard laughs at Duke's article saying he wrote 'Mood Indigo' in fifteen minutes while his mother made breakfast, when Bigard says he gave Duke the last half and Duke added the first.

segments.title: Ellington's men who wrote tunes and never got credit
segments.summary: Hodges, Brown, Hardwick, Cootie and Rex wrote numbers that went out under Duke's and Irving Mills's names for $25 or $50 and by the time they learned better it was too late.

segments.title: Duke's real talent: hearing riffs and writing to fit each man
segments.summary: Bigard says Duke's talent was creative ideas and studying each player so his writing fit like a glove, turning solo riffs into new tunes, unlike Calloway, and Tyree Glenn says he listened to new men for two months.

segments.title: Tricky Sam gets his solo and the growl of 'Black and Tan Fantasy'
segments.summary: Duke ignored Tricky Sam Nanton until Otto Hardwick insisted; the growl duets with Bubber Miley came from the men and Duke wrote 'Black and Tan Fantasy' for them.

segments.title: The Ellington sound on radio and working through the Depression
segments.summary: You could tell it was Ellington within seconds on radio, and the band worked everywhere through the Depression while others starved.

segments.title: Alabama theater where Black audiences were afraid to applaud
segments.summary: In an Alabama white theater the manager set aside one day for Black patrons, who packed the house and tapped their feet but dared not applaud.

segments.title: Whether Ellington ever took a stand on segregation
segments.summary: Bigard says Duke never spoke out while he was with him, even though he called Jump for Joy a social statement, unlike Louis, who spoke up about Faubus.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong's outspokenness and the alligator story
segments.summary: Louis said whatever he wished, even in the South, such as telling Tommy Dorsey 'not too slow, not too fast, just half-ass' on TV and telling a concert audience a joke about an alligator.

segments.title: Ellington's brief open solo spaces
segments.summary: Duke's arrangements left a bare space marked 'solo' of eight or sixteen bars, with no time to settle in on an original tune.

segments.title: Woodshedding modern tunes after leaving Duke
segments.summary: After years of only Duke's tunes he had to learn everyday songs, which gave him broader experience; now he will play any kind of music for money.

segments.title: Harry Carney's baritone, stiff reed and playing seated
segments.summary: Carney played baritone while Hardwick played bass sax when Bigard joined; he used a very stiff reed and played sitting because it was easier to manipulate.

segments.title: Band nicknames: Posey, Sweetie, Dumpy and Cutie
segments.summary: Freddie Jenkins was called Posey for posing, Lawrence Brown Sweetie for powdering his face, and Duke Dumpy and Cutie; Woodyard still calls him Piano Red.

segments.title: Pranks on Posey and Art Whetsol
segments.summary: The band put limburger cheese and cayenne pepper in Posey's mouthpiece and swapped Art Whetsol's valves around.

segments.title: Soaping the fiddle bow of prima donna Ada Ward
segments.summary: When Cotton Club singer Ada Ward tried to get the band fired, Otto Hardwick soaped the violinist's bow so her obbligato made no sound and she walked off crying.

segments.title: Water in Braud's tuba
segments.summary: The band poured two buckets of water down Braud's tuba, and Bigard, sitting beneath him, got drenched when Duke made him play it.

segments.title: Tizol's stink bomb during 'Mood Indigo' in Philadelphia
segments.summary: They toothpicked Bigard's keys, and in a hot Philadelphia theater Tizol burst a stink bomb during the 'Mood Indigo' trio so that Bigard and Tricky blamed each other and left Whetsol playing alone.

segments.title: Itching powder in Tizol's shirt
segments.summary: Bigard and Hodges got revenge by dusting Tizol's shirt sleeve with itching powder, so he left the stand and gave up pranks.

segments.title: Billy Strayhorn first meets Duke
segments.summary: Bigard remembers Strayhorn as brilliant and nice, and says he first met Duke on a train in Pittsburgh.

segments.title: The Mills Brothers' audition on Duke's train
segments.summary: Duke's manager discouraged him from hearing the Mills Brothers, who auditioned on the train, and another agent took them and made the money that should have been Duke's.

segments.title: Strayhorn starts by writing out Duke's arrangements
segments.summary: Strayhorn began copying out Duke's compositions when Tizol's extraction work became too much, learned how Duke worked and would not sell his secrets, which Duke liked.

segments.title: George Gershwin wanted to collaborate with Duke
segments.summary: Bigard says Gershwin proposed a songwriting partnership from the Cotton Club days and Duke refused, wanting to do it all himself.

segments.title: Los Angeles in 1942: Central Avenue clubs and swampy Watts
segments.summary: Bigard names the Cotton Club and Club Alabam on Central Avenue, remembers Watts as swampland where he went crawfishing, and says after-hours spots there were mostly hustling for rent.

segments.title: Downtown Los Angeles theaters: the Pantages and the Million Dollar
segments.summary: They sort out the Orpheum and Pantages downtown theaters with stage-show bands, and Bigard worked one with Freddie Slack that later became the Million Dollar.

segments.title: Billy Berg's and the small Los Angeles clubs
segments.summary: Billy Berg's was the best small club, with Teddy Bunn, Leo Watson, Slim Gaillard, Nellie Lutcher and Harry the Hipster Gibson.

segments.title: Local bands: Les Hite with Lawrence Brown and Lionel Hampton
segments.summary: Les Hite had a big band here with Lawrence Brown and Lionel Hampton; otherwise not much musically was going on.

segments.title: Putting Kid Ory in his band at Billy Berg's Capri
segments.summary: Bigard hired a down-and-out Ory, who had worked for his uncle in New Orleans and was getting $12 a week, with Red Mack and Charlie Mingus, and Ory stole the show with 'Muskrat Ramble' and 'Ory's Creole Trombone'.

segments.title: Getting Kid Ory his Muskrat Ramble royalties
segments.summary: Learning Ory never saw royalties, Bigard traced the song from Melrose to publisher John Levy, who gave Ory a check for about $8,500, then $700 each quarter; Bigard says Ellington and Mills had tricked him.

segments.title: Why Bigard cannot recover back royalties on 'Mood Indigo'
segments.summary: Willard asks why there is no retroactive money; Bigard says Mills and Ellington were already paid, that his name was missing for 28 years, and that he has thirteen tunes there.

segments.title: Recording the 'Easy on the Ear' album for RCA
segments.summary: He has five new tunes on his latest record, issued first in France; royalties come only after about a year.

segments.title: How his name reached 'Mood Indigo' and the ASCAP three-hit rule
segments.summary: His name got onto 'Mood Indigo' after the 28th year when it was reissued; ASCAP required three hits for membership until BMI began buying numbers.

segments.title: Publishers shelving tunes and then releasing them under their own names
segments.summary: Publishers asked for submissions, put them on the shelf for years and then published them under the company's name, so people now publish their own music.

segments.title: 'Clarinet Gumbo', Easy on the Ear and Mickey Goldstein's plans
segments.summary: Willard has the RCA album titled 'Clarinet Gumbo', the French title being 'Easy on the Ear'; Bigard is not under contract, and manager Mickey Goldstein wants Duke-style numbers.

segments.title: The discography compiled by a French doctor
segments.summary: Dr. Kochlin of Paris gave him a discography running from 1926 to the sixties, with first recording in 1926 with Luis Russell and sessions with Jelly Roll Morton and Johnny Dodds, and tunes he had forgotten.

segments.title: The early recording process and Bigard's first Ellington 'Bugle Call Rag'
segments.summary: Early records used horns gathered in one bunch with no bass or drums, and he has never found his first Ellington record, 'Bugle Call Rag', from about January 1928.

segments.chapter: Ellington band: drinking, quarrels and rent parties
segments.title: End of reel five and start of reel six
segments.summary: Reel five ends and the reel six header and proceedings begin.

segments.chapter: Ellington band: drinking, quarrels and rent parties
segments.title: Sonny Greer's drinking and the Kansas City druggist's fake drink
segments.summary: Duke had a Kansas City druggist serve Sonny a fake drink, which made Sonny pass out anyway; Bigard adds that Sonny had a phenomenal memory for names.

segments.chapter: Ellington band: drinking, quarrels and rent parties
segments.title: Whether Duke drank, and the rent parties
segments.summary: Duke was not a heavy drinker in Bigard's time; the rent parties, or chitlin switches, served the world's worst bathtub gin.

segments.chapter: Ellington band: drinking, quarrels and rent parties
segments.title: How Ben Webster got Bigard drinking and telling Duke off
segments.summary: He did not drink until he saw Ben Webster curse Duke without answer, so he began on sherry with Johnny Hodges's wife and told Duke off all the time.

segments.chapter: Ellington band: drinking, quarrels and rent parties
segments.title: Who Duke left alone: Brown, Tizol and Tricky Sam
segments.summary: Duke liked people who talked back; Lawrence Brown never did and was never close to him, while Tizol and Tricky Sam told him to leave them alone.

segments.chapter: Ellington band: drinking, quarrels and rent parties
segments.title: Ivie Anderson, Cootie Williams and the gun in El Paso
segments.summary: Cootie hit Ivie Anderson in the head with a window jack during a train card game; she bought a gun in El Paso, but Duke cooled it and the two ended up together.

segments.chapter: Ellington band: drinking, quarrels and rent parties
segments.title: Cutting contests rather than jam sessions, and his debut at Mexico's
segments.summary: Horn players did not play rent parties; cutting contests at Mexico's in the basement had a night for each instrument, and that was Bigard's New York debut before he went to the Nest.

segments.title: What early records were made on
segments.summary: Asked about hot wax, he says New York used the same process as now.

segments.title: Recording with King Oliver while with Duke; never under contract
segments.summary: He recorded with Oliver for Clarence Williams after joining Duke, and says he was never under contract to Duke, who could fire him at will as in the early days.

segments.title: Oliver's band stranded in Baltimore, then Milwaukee with Elgar
segments.summary: The band got stranded in Baltimore, Bigard ate hot dogs and then cabbage for days, then Omer Simeon wrote Charlie Elgar and Bigard spent months in Milwaukee before Luis Russell sent for him in New York.

segments.title: The Oliver date that was really for Clarence Williams
segments.summary: Williams, who Bigard calls a big crook who stole 'Sister Kate' from Piron, could not get Buster Bailey and got Bigard to record on a date he thought was Oliver's.

segments.title: Ellington sessions of January to March 1928
segments.summary: Willard reads the discography for 'Bugle Call Rag', 'Take It Easy' and 'Jubilee Stomp'; Bigard says the process allowed only a snare drum, not a bass drum, and recalls the band's personnel.

segments.title: Recording with Jelly Roll Morton in 1929
segments.summary: Bigard recorded with anyone who wanted him and paid him, including Jelly Roll in 1929 while with Duke.

segments.title: Small-group recordings under Ellington sidemen's names
segments.summary: Sessions credited to Sonny Greer and His Memphis Men, Barney and His Stinkopatsers or Rex Stewart's Rextet used Duke's players under other names because Duke was under contract.

segments.title: Films in the discography: 'Bundle of Blues' and 'Belle of the Nineties'
segments.summary: Willard asks about early films; he does not recall 'Bundle of Blues' and identifies 'Belle of the Nineties' as Mae West's film.

segments.title: Louis introduces an African woman as his mother
segments.summary: On a government goodwill tour of Africa before a crowd of over 100,000, Louis called an unknown African woman up to meet his mother.

segments.title: Taking a cab to the park to stick manager Frenchie with the fare
segments.summary: When manager Frenchie Pierre Tallerie left without him, Bigard took a cab to the park and pointed Frenchie out to the driver to be paid.

segments.title: A lizard in the hotel wall in Africa
segments.summary: Bigard fled a hotel room when a large lizard came through the wall and was told it eats mosquitoes, then slept on a bar bench.

segments.title: Playing under guard during the Mau Mau fighting in the Congo
segments.summary: On the 1959-60 tour, soldiers and bowmen ringed the hotel veranda where they played for dignitaries, so Bigard stayed behind the piano; he says the war stopped while Louie was there.

segments.title: Leopard men on the road in the French Cameroons
segments.summary: A French patrol turned them back one rainy night because leopard men were out to kill; Bigard also warns that calling an African 'Bwana' invites violence.

segments.title: African cities, American-style music and coconut drying
segments.summary: They toured all over Africa; the cities were modern, local bands tried to play American music while tribal drumming was separate, and he saw green coconuts laid out in the sun beside ships waiting to load.

segments.title: Recording in France and England; the later session with Claude Luter
segments.summary: Bigard has been to France several times and recorded in France and England only with Louie and Duke until Mrs. Bigard recalls a later record with Claude Luter around 1960.

segments.title: Kay Starr date in 1945 and Ted Yerxa's Lamplighter records
segments.summary: He recorded in Los Angeles with Willie Smith, Ray Linn, Calvin Jackson and Zutty, and Ted Yerxa of the Lamplighter, a Daily News columnist, put many musicians to work recording, including Vic Dickenson and Peggy Lee.

segments.title: Other 1945-46 sessions: Wini Beatty, Charlie Ventura and Benny Carter
segments.summary: Willard reads discography entries from 1945-46 with Wini Beatty, Claude Trenier, Charlie Ventura, Louis Armstrong and Benny Carter, which Mrs. Bigard says were all Ted Yerxa dates.

segments.title: The 1962 Benny Carter, Ben Webster and Barney Bigard record
segments.summary: The BBB date in April 1962 was Leonard Feather's, and Bigard recorded it sick with a 104 fever.

segments.title: Recordings with Armstrong and Hines: film, Switzerland, Paris and the Crescendo
segments.summary: They go through the film 'New Orleans' music, a 1949 Empire Room broadcast, concerts in Switzerland and Trieste, Paris with Earl Hines and Buck Clayton, and the 1962 session; he only started keeping his records ten years ago.

segments.title: The 'Clarinet Gumbo' release and the planned Pelican Trio album
segments.summary: His new album comes out in Europe and then the United States as 'Clarinet Gumbo'; another, with Barry Martyn and Duke Burrell recorded in Vienna, will be called the Pelican Trio after the Pelican State.

segments.title: 'Crawfish Blues' royalties of 49 cents and the unfinished Pelican Trio record
segments.summary: His blues with Zutty, called 'Crawfish Blues', earned him 49 cents after sixteen years from Mickey Goldsen, and the last Pelican Trio session got hung up and is unfinished.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
segments.title: The Satchmo tribute at the Wilshire Ebell and Joe Venuti
segments.summary: He describes his September engagement, a three-night tribute to Louis Armstrong with Trummy Young, Teddy Buckner and Cozy Cole, plus a blues night with John Lee Hooker and a night featuring Joe Venuti.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
segments.title: Big Sid Catlett, his all-time favorite drummer
segments.summary: Bigard says Big Sid never played show-off paradiddles, his solos echoed the tune's theme, he kept time like the Rock of Gibraltar, and he would tune his drums during the theme song.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
segments.title: Louis Armstrong's generosity and Stuff Crouch's club
segments.summary: Louis gave money to everyone, including Stuff Crouch, whom he set up with an after-hours club and a big Chrysler, and Crouch charged the band when they came over; Louis paid for Crouch's funeral.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
segments.title: Louis and the baby that was not his
segments.summary: Louis saved coins in a bag for the child of a woman who claimed he was the father, and Lucille told him he could not have fathered a child, which Bigard offers to show how easily he was fooled.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
segments.title: Joe Glaser as Armstrong's manager and how he bought his contract
segments.summary: Glaser did not pay Louis's bills; he bought Louis's contract for $500 from a man who had beaten him, took abuse from Southerners for working with Black musicians, and Louis called him his father.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
segments.title: Glaser's salary and the IOU slips that kept Louis solvent
segments.summary: Louis had worked at Glaser's Sunset Cafe in Chicago before Erskine Tate, and Glaser put him on a salary with IOUs checked afterwards because his big heart gave everything away.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
segments.title: Dicky Wells drinks the money for his fare home at the first Nice festival
segments.summary: At the first Nice festival, the band and Louie collected money to send a trombonist home, but he drank it and was still in France; Bigard names Dicky Wells.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
segments.title: Dicky Wells working Louis for $25 above the Turf in New York
segments.summary: Bigard overheard Dicky Wells boast to a friend that he would show him how to get money, then win $25 from Louis with a sad story.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
segments.title: Louis wrecks his Plymouth and the tea he smoked
segments.summary: Louis, high on tea, ran into a bus and planned to give the wrecked car to his sister; Bigard says Crouch got him brick marijuana from Mexico, and Cozy Cole nearly crushed Louis's head after a racial insult in Europe.

segments.title: End of reel six and start of reel seven, July 5
segments.summary: Reel six ends, and Willard opens reel seven on July 5 to follow up earlier questions.

segments.title: Octave Gaspard and his brothers
segments.summary: The bandleader was Octave Gaspard, who got lots of jobs; his brother Vic played trombone, and they were the important ones because they got the work.

segments.title: King Oliver's trombonist George Fields and trumpeter Bob Schaffner
segments.summary: Bigard names the missing members of Oliver's band, George Fields and Bob Schaffner, who stayed in Chicago and had a lip pierced.

segments.title: King Oliver's pyorrhea and the origin of the qua-qua mute
segments.summary: Oliver's bad teeth often kept him from playing; he got his mute sounds with his hand, and Paddy Harmon had someone copy it and sold a similar 'qua-qua' mute without paying Oliver.

segments.title: Follow-up on the comedians and 'Rocking in Rhythm'
segments.summary: He still cannot name Johnny Lee's partner but says he and Hodges thought up the ditty, Duke made the tune, and Carney's name on it is a joke.

segments.title: Correcting the 'Clarinet Gumbo' liner notes on his father and Tom Anderson's
segments.summary: Willard reads the liner notes; Bigard says his father was no musician, the violinist was his uncle Emile, and that he joined Albert Nicholas's group at Tom Anderson's.

segments.title: 'Dreamy Blues', 'C Jam Blues' and which tunes were his
segments.summary: He denies writing 'C Jam Blues' and lets Europeans think so; 'Saturday Night Function' and 'Stompy Jones' are right, and he recorded it first with his small group.

segments.title: Honors: Who's Who, key to New Orleans and the Mood Indigo Hall of Fame
segments.summary: Mrs. Bigard lists his Who's Who entry since 1949, the 1972 New Orleans key to the city from Mayor Landrieu and a plaque, and the Hall of Fame award for songwriting 'Mood Indigo'.

segments.title: French television biography filmed by J. C. Averty
segments.summary: Last year in France he was filmed for a French TV musical biography directed by J. C. Averty, though the release may take years.

segments.title: Newport Hall of Fame and the disc from the mayor of Nice
segments.summary: Last year George Wein gave him a first Newport Hall of Fame award among eleven musicians, and the mayor of Nice gave him a Latin disc.

segments.title: Esquire awards and closing remarks
segments.summary: He holds three Esquire silver awards in the years Benny Goodman won gold, and says he is still working for more.
